IN WINTER.

When winter skies are clear and cold And trees are hung with frosty laces, Beside the embers--growing old— We sit and dream of far off faces. The year is dying—all is snow— We only think 011 long ago. Across the silence of the years We stretch our hands with sudden yearning ; With eves all dim—through unshed tears— We look to see old friends returning. But never touch of vanished hand Shall greet us from the shadow land. They passed and left no footprints here, The snows of time have hid their traces, We only hold their memory dear— Keep in our hearts their empty places. Their looks, their words, a tender store—. But they will come no more—no more! Oh I warm young hands, like sun kissed flow'rs, Still in your loving guidance hold us! Young eyes—look tenderly in ours! Young hearts—in All your joys enfold us! Go swiftly; gladly forth to greet The coming year—'tis dawning sweet, We follow on your eager feet. —From "Fun Almanac."

HOW. KATHLEEN O'HONE DECLINED THE MARRIED STATE. Sure, its ahll the bhoys in Kilobrienstown (an' ivvery sowl that clapped ois on her, for the matter o' that) were jist madly in love wid that Rathlane O'Hone. An', be the sowl o' me Sunday brogues she was an illigant shlip of a craythur, annyway. But nivver so much as a blink of her purthy oi could she cyast on anny wan o' them, barrin' Andy McShane, as loikely a bhoy as anny colleen need be lookun' for—an' mebbe not foind um , When An' be the same token, it's as thick as thayves they were before you could say " shebeen," with army knowludge of the manin' av it, an' in a wake's toime sure its Andy himself was afther goun' the len'th o' Father Dan's, and Misthress O'Hone began turrin' out the linen chist, an' handin' over illigant hape of ut tor Rathlane. An' it's moighty shov she was, the crayther, ahll the toime, blushun' an' runnun' away to hoide her- silf evvery minut ; but ye could see the happiness of her, the darlint, sparklin' in her ois, an' tickliif the earners of her mouth into dimples an' schmoiles. But wan day, bad luck to ut Kathlane was takin' a walk, whin she came up by Rory McGrath's cabin, and if Eileen McGrath (divil fly away wid her!) wasn't' shtandin' at the dure, nursing her last pair o' shqualin' twins, wid the other pair foightin' in front av her. NOT A GRONMETTFIES. When first the steam tramway car ran in our town it was regarded by the working population much in the light of a private carriage, to await their individual will and pleasure, as the following anecdote will show. An old:woman, seated in one of the cars, suddenly motioned the guard to stop, at the same time beckoning to a child on the sidewalk. In obedience to the signal the latter entered the car, was rapturously embraced, and sum- marily dismissed. Indignant at the wanton waste of his own and the other passengeriftime,the guard strongly remonstrated with the old body upon her extraordinary "- conduct, but was answered by the withering remark, " It's easy to see as tha's never bin' a grorximeyther. Aw think more o' you lass than a't trams int wand !" A "BATTLE' AT." At a review of some of our local Volunteers some con- • fusion was observed in the ranks of one of the companies, and on the captain inquiring the cause, he recived the following explanation; "Whey it's Bill Harrud ! It's nobbut lost it battle'at !'" A CBUSIIING REPLY. It is an accepted fact that the "getting up" of rallies at a bazaar is a most wearisome and thankless undertaking, and that the repulses sometimes met with are hard to bear, not to say crushing, as was the follow- ing. While dilating on the qualities of the offered article, the railer explained its value in being a piece of genuine art—" It is hand-painted." "Aye, au' so's eawr back dur 1" was the dry reply. div.p: CHRISTMAS CURIOUSLY KEPT.

CHRISTMAS IN THE CLOUDS. But we will quit the sea, and you—my friend,of the roast beef and pudding—shall come with me for a little jaunt to the top of Ben Nevis. Knew you, pere.hance,l that in this, the best mountain that Nature can do for us, ay, and a decent mountain, too, there is an observa- tory never left; that night by night and year by year the astronomers there are gazing at the stars, turning old Jupiter and the planets inside out, inquiring after the health of the moon, and asking comets what they mean by it. These men, indeed, do spend a curious Christmas: the road to the lower ground is blocked by the masses of snow that cover it; and often enough even the very observatory runs a danger of being engulfed in tke fleecy falls that sweep upon the summit. No, our friends the astronomers are prisoners if you like; often cut off for weeks, and yet merry in their way in the little house that caps the mount. There the struggling traveller, who reaches the altitude when the weather is a little kinder, is entertained right heartily. steaming coffee brings back circulation to the frozen fin- gers, a roaring fire melts the ice on the clinging cape ; there is food and shelter ad lib. in the home of the star- g,asers, 'who celebrate Christmss merrily enough, with plenteou* fare, bright fires, and the peculiar satisfaction that they are where no men can c(- me to them. SOME ODD CHRISTMASES. I have often thought that the late Colonel Burnaby passed some Very curious Christmas Days. What more outrageous to our notions than to celebrate the great feast in the very heart of the snowclad Russiati plains by Oxenburg ; to be skimming in a sledge., a little Tar- tar servant vowing that he could go no farther; to be at length turned out in the snow, &I'd to sleep exposed to those terrible winds of EasternEussia ? Do you remem- ber the Colonel's own description? "There was no wood in the neighbourhood, nothing with which we could make a fire; and the sleeping-sack, which I at once thought of, proved useless, owing to the small size of the aperture. We had no shOvel to make a snow-house, and there was nought to do save to it it out the livelong night. "My hands and feet first began to smart, and the nails to ache as they were being scorched over a fire—a nasty, burning, gnawing sensation, which ate into the joints, and then died away in a dull feeling of indescribable numbness which seized all my limbs. A heavy weight seemed to bear me down. and I dozed of for a second, till aroused once mare to the reality of ezistence by the groaning of my little servant. He was murmuring some- thing to himself in a low tone, but not one word of com- plaint ever escaped his lips. "There was soon no more pain; and my thoughts began to wander to far-off places, whilst well-known faces came and looked at me, then flitted away in the waste, and were replaced by well spread banquet-balls, laden with viands which vanished as in my dream I strove to partake. At last the dream was over, and I was lost to consciousness,when I was aroused by a sharp tap on the elbow and a violent shaking from the hands of my follower. •Do not close your eyes, sir,' he said, 4 or you will never open them again.'" —From "Answers."

-- - CONUNDRUMS. nat metamorphosis will the Prince of Wales undergo, and what sacrifice will he make, on coming to the throne 7—He will be changed into a sovereign, and give tip his title for a crown. Why is the letter N like a halfpenny 7—Because there are two of them in a penny. What portion of the day does the letter U re- semble 7—Evening ; because it comes after T. What carpenter's tool is like a dish for cooling tea 7—Saw, sir (saucer). What town in Ireland reminds one of a candle just burning out 7—Wicklow. Why was the first day of Adam's life the longest ever known ?—Because it had no Eve. Why is absenc3 like a pair of bellows 2—Because it strengthens a strong claim and extinguishes a weak one. What portions of an elephant would remind you of a state in Italy ?—Tusk-and-eye (Tuscany). Why should railway travellers invariably avoid the 12.50 train 7—Because it is 10 to 1 if they catch it. When may a young lady in love be said to have put her foot in it 7—When sly.: has drawn her stocking on. Why ought the letters of the alphabet to he re- arranged 7 Because many of them are out of "order." What garment does a coat become when you've one wearing it 7—A waistcoat (waste). Why was William the Conqueror after a good dinner like a spoilt child 7—Because he was wilful (Will full). What part of a river resembles pride 7—That which " goea before a fall." What -bird would make a pedlar 7—Hawk. When is a bow not a bow 7—When it is a knot. Why is a waterman like a red herring 7—Be- cause it has often a hard roe (row). What poet had temporal and spiritual authority in his day 2—Pope. Why is a man in a rage like a hard-baked pie —Because he is crusty. How many peas are there in a pint 2—One P. Why are soldiers more tired on the first of April than on other days of the year 7—Because thy have gone through a March of 31 days. What dish furnishes the best conversation ? Tongue and brains. What is the ditlerence betwen a special constable and a superannuated constable 7--The former's sworn in, the latter's worn out. What is that from which, if you take the whole, some will remain 7—The word wholesome: What is the difference between an honest and a dishonest laundress 7—The former irons your linen, the latter steals it. , Wipe my face and Pm everybody, scratch my back and I'm nobody. What is it ?—A mirror.

The most elaborate of the Christmas cards have a box to themselves. Here is one with a gate, standing off the body of the card, on which are perched robins and other feathered songsters, the whole making a bright and pretty winter scene. Another has at first glance all the apprarance of " a silken valentine," but an in- vestigation into its mysteries reveals three wonderfully finished moonlight scenes with the customary season's wishes. One card is made so that it will stand alone, and, by way of contrast to winter, reproduces a har- vest scene so perfectly as to take in its suggestiveness something of the chill off the weather. There are sets of of private autograph and other cards of the most novel design ; some folding cards and some single flowers, birds and beast being requisitioned to add to the effect. One large card is mounted with a flock of birds which look so natural that the spectator would hardly be sur- prised if they commenced to sing. Amongst the most elegant are some with landscapes v.gnettes,so eloborately finished as to defy criticism. The figure cards are of the nattiest kind, comical, but they are not at all vulgar. Every fancy may be said to be met ; for every class seems to have been considered. They must be beyond pleasing, who, geing to a stationer's shop, and inspect- ing Messrs. Tuck and Sons productions, fail to find some- thing exactly to their taste. Their cards and booklets for the present season may in fact be said to indicate the high-water mark of art in this particular channA.

------• It was early evening ere Zenobie entered the apartment of her voting mistress. As she opened the door she found all dark within. She moved into the room, and shading her candle with her hand she gazed about. The wind still howled fearfully with- out, and the snow catne driving against the win- dow's. When the girl had reached the extremity of the place she called her mistress's name, and she was answered by a low groan from the couch in the corner. Thither she hastened, and there she found her mistress.
".Rosalind—my mistress !" she cried, kneeling down.

"Who is it?' the maiden asked, starting up, and gazing frantically around. "It is me, Zenobie. Say, my dear, good mistress —what is it? What is the matter? What has happened?" With a quick movement Rosalind put her attend- ant away and sat up; and having gazed about her for some moments she murmured: "Where am I ? who is here?"

"It is I. You are in your own chamber. Come —you are cold here," Without resistence the maiden suffered herself to be led to the place where the heated air came up from the furnace below, and there she sat down. " What is it ?" again asked Zenobie, eagerly. " What has happened ?" Rosalind bowed her head upon her hands, and after some moments of thought she looked up, She was very pale, and a fearful tremor shook her frame. " Zenobie," she uttered, in a low, strange whisper. " Ask me no more now. lam not well. Oh, ask me no more now." " My mistress," returned the faithful girl, placing one arm about Rosalind's neck, "you know what you may tell me, and what you may not; but whom will you trust if you trust not me? Oh, give me your love, and if I can serve you let me do so." " I would trust you with life itself," the maiden lw all that
has happened here ; but not now— cannot speak it now! " Say no more, my mistress ; only let me serve you. You will hare some refreshment—something to eat."

"You may bring me some wine, Zenobie.' And thereupon the young girl hastened away. In the meantime the duke was in his private room below. He was pacing to and fro across the floor with his hands behind him, and his brow was dark and lowering. Ever and anon he would stop near the door and listen, and then proceed. At length there came a rap upon the door, and the duke said, "Enter." It was a priest who entered the apart- ment—a small, deformed man, somewhere about fifty years of age. His face was very dark ; his features sharp and and angular; his eves dark, and sunken deep into his head ; his brow heavy above the eyes, where the shaggy brows hung over, but sloping back from thence, leaving the points where phrenologists locate benevolence and veneration deficient and flat. Upon his shoulders he wore a huge, ungainly hump; and, all in all, be was just such a man as a timid person would shun. His name was Savotano. The duke had been the means of getting him into the church, and in considera- tion thereof he had bound himself to do the duke's evil work. But this is not all. - .

Some years before there had been a murder in Moscow, and Savotano did the bloody deed. It was a work of pure vengeance. Olga had him appre- hended ; but he was not brought to justice. The duke found him to be a shrewd, unscrupulous wretch, willing to servo those who would pay him well, and ready to let himself then to any one who could save his life. Olga was a man of plots and schemes. He fancied that such a man as Savotano might be of use to him; so he proposed to save him if he would serve his benefactor. The villain was glad enough to accept the proposition, and the bar- gain was made. Could Savotano enter the church, and assume the sacred garb, he might in many cases work to better advantage. The wretch readily agreed to this, too ; and through Olga's powerful in- fluence he gained a place in the church. He knew that the duke held his very life, and he failed not to serve him. His clerical robes shielded him from ; much suspicion; and, moreover, the place gave him additional advantages to work at his diabolical trade. His salary from the government was sufficient for hie support, while an occasional sum from his master enabled him to enjoy many of those luxuries which were denied to most of his brethren. Olga feared not to trust this man, for the fellow had nothing to gain by betrayal but everything to lose. And such was the man who now entered the duke's private room. Ile entered with a bold air, for though he was somewhat in the duke's power, yet there was a peculiar satisfaction in knowing that when he fell the noble lord must fall with him, part way, at least. Brethren in crime cannot count much upon respect. "I have come, my lord,' the priest said as he shook the snow from his robe, and then took a seat by the furnace-pipe. "And how is the count ?" asked Olga. :1 " Ile is recovering, I am sure." "Does Kopani say so ?" " Yes. He says he will have him out within a month." " By heavens, Savotano, this must not be. "But tell me, my lord,what is the particular need of the count's departing ?" The duke gazed his visitor a few moments in the face, and then he said: " Why since the affair interests you, I'll tell you. Thus far I have paid you promptly all your dues, but I cannot do so much longer unless we can make some of our points work. ly property is on the decrease fast. I have not enough left to live on. Within the past three years I have made some bad ventures. I put into—but never mind—suffice it for me to say that I am at the end of my for- tune." The duke was about to say that he had placed large sums in the hands of the Minister Galitzin for the purpose of carrying out the conspiracy by which the Princess Sophia was to have been placed upon the throne, with Galitzin for her prime minister, and himself also high in power. He chose not to tell of this—and no wonder, for heads had ere then been taken to pay for such indiscretions: "And now if this count survives I thus have one source cut off. My half of Drotzen is used up and mortgaged to him, but if he dies the whole comes to me. His father and myself married sisters, and they owned Drotzen, and on his side the Count is the only heir; so in the event of his death the whole comes to me. You understand this now." "Perfectly," returned the priest. "And 'tis a pity your first effort did not succeed." "So it is," said the duke uneasily. "When I sent him with that message tone gun-maker I felt sure he would be slain, and then I hoped that the other could be disposed of for having slain him. But the Emperor has turned all my plans upside down, for the present at least. Savotano, you must have a hand in Damonoff's medicine !" "That is easily done, my lord," replied the priest quietly. "You have free access there ?" "Yes." "And can you not watch with him some night ?" "I think I can."
diall kno —not now. Oho I lirom RODIO

" Wh'v—l think he is a spy of the Pope—sent hero irom Rome to learn something of our Emperor's plans." "But he has not visited the imperial palace." "Oh yes, my lord. He has been there several times ; and once the Emperor himself was obliged to send him out of the audience chamber." "But have you any particular reasons for think- ing him a spy from the Pope ? " "Why—he is a Romish monk; and he hangs about the most important places in the city. Even the circumstances I have just related—his trying to re- main in the audience chamber while private bust- I ness was going on. and having to be ordered out by the Emperor—is some ground for suspicion. I mean ' to watch him at all events." "That's right," returned the duke. And then, , after a moment's thought, he added: Ido not see why he should be around after every petty duel that may be fought, if he is a spy from Rome. And besides I have heard one or two persons say that they were sure they had seen him before." "Oh. that may be only the result of some strong resemblance which he bears to someone else. I ant sure he was never here before—not in Moscow." Again the hump-backed priest was cautioned about the work he had in hand,and having promised over and over again to be very careful, lie took 1115 t leave. And Olga, Duke of Tula, was left alone with ' his own thoughts. Better for him had that wicked priest been his executioner ! Better for him had be been upon the count's bed, racked with dying pains! Better for him had he been a poor gun-maker, so he Lad been honest! Oh, better for him had he been the meanest beggar that walked the earth, thou, what he was! But he did not realize this. He had a goal ahead, and he tried to overlook the black, dreadful gulf that yawned between him and it I bar- (To be continued.)

[Published by Mr. John Heywood, Manchester,:as a Penny Reading.] Mn. PETER Purii!LAN was wider book-keeper at Millbrock Mill, a post which he had occupied at the period we write of for fifteen weeks. It wail his function to weigh out" twist "to the winders, Make up wages, and do the booking generally for the warpers, loomers, and tapers. Mr. Peter Penman was a little man with a little post, but in his:own estimation he was in everything very great. He was just nineteen years of age, but he spoke upon everything with the air of a man who had in that brief period concentrated the experience and wis- dom of ninety. Mr. Peter had, therefore, a great amount of assurance. He was possessed likewise of a considerable stock of slang, which he mistook for wit; of a variety of collars and ties of the latest style; of a meerschaum, which he had coloured beautifully ; and, last and least, of a bit of down at each corner of his mouth, which he had dignified with the appellation of moustache. It was within three days of Christmas, and Mr. Peter had received a note from Messrs. Perkins & Co., a firm that supplied his employers with flour for sizing, intimating that if he would call upon Mr. Turnspit, the poulterer, he would find a couple of rabbits and a goose (or turkey, if preferred), which were placed at the disposal of himself and friends. "Ah ! very good! capital ! " said Mr. Peter as he re-read the letter, and made sundry ineffectual at- tempts with his thumb and torefinger at twisting the afore-mentioned down at the afore-mentioned corners of his mouth. "This is one of the per- quisites, is it ?—a compliment to those who under- stand a thing or two. And very proper, too. ; Per- kins' know what they're about; but I shouldn't wonder if Kit and the tapers will have cheek enough to want to go snacks; but not me; catch me at it, that's all." It should be stated that Kit was his factotum- his general general assistant. Kit was about forty years of age, tall, thin, and muscular. Ile had a keen, hungry look, as if he was constantly expecting ai good dinner, which, somehow, never arrived. -His chief characteristic, however, was his unfortunate habit of stammering, so that he was sometimes referred to, by way of distinction, ai " Stutting Kit." ' Hav- ing been many years about the premises, and being noted for his industry, he was somewhat of a favourite with his masters, and thus privileged at times to play practical jokes upon his fellow-opera- tives. Kit was a handy man, too; he could, with the aid of a steam-hoist, empty a cart or lurry of its load of yarn in a remarkably short space of time; and was good at anything—from making shoddy- bags to flanging a weaver's beam. On the par- ticular morning referred -to he looked more than usually keen and hungry.. He knew something of Christmas perquisites; had hitherto always enjoyed a share in what he called " th' fleawr brass;" and had, in fact, so sharp an eye te the possible contents of each envelope, that he was at hand by the time Mr. Peter had read his letter and finished his little soliloquy. "Here's a "go ! " said Peter. "Perkins' have sent me a turkey and a couple of rabbits; at least I can have 'em for fetching,' "Nay, sure ! " exclaimed Kit, " th-tha 'never says soa! Wod dun they say ? " " Oh, here it is," said Peter, turning to the letter —" 'a goose or turkey, whichever you prefer, and a couple of rabbits, which we have placed at the dis- posal of yourself and friends.' Now, for my part, I say turkey—turkey's the word. Everybody has goose at Christmas—awfully common and niuniA- - or tor ey, it's o th' same to me ; it'll be a rare b-b-blow eawt, that's: one c-c-comfort— 'specially if we put abeawt a shilling a-piece to it. Aw could H-just-40-usaw—wi-a-leg-aze--. a; bit o'th' breast." "A leg and a bit of the breast! Coirle, that's good for you, Kit; but don't you wish you may get it ? " "Well, awse g-g-ged mi sh-share, a , expect. There'll only be f-t-five on us—th-three tapers an us two. Egad! there'll j-j-just be two legs apiece eawt o' two rapputs an' a torkey." "Look you here, cheeky," snarled Peter, "these things are for me—me, stupid; and as for you and the tapers, why you can just jump up for what you call your share.' "Nay, hang id, Peter ! Tha n-n-never meons thad. It's b-b-bad enough to rob a poor m-m-man of his beer, as song says; but t-t-to take meyt eawt of his m-m-meawth, it's as ill as k-k-killing a paason." "Why, what are you talking about, Kit? Don't you understand plain English? Perkins' have write ten to me: it's for me and my friends. You don't mean to say that has any reference to you and the tapers? " "And w-why nod ?" said Kit. "It alus has had aw c-c-con tell thi." " Ha, ha, ha! well done, Kit ! By Joie you're the funniest fellow out. You class yourself as one of my friends. Ha, ha, ha! The scavengers will be claiming my acquaintance next. By Jingol /his is a joke. Really, I shall die laughing. But you don't come over me in that style ;it may do for your raw recruits, but not foryour old soldier—oh, dear no!" "Then tha d-d-doesn't meon to be j-j-jannock—to share an' share alike abeawt them rapputs and torkey ? " "I shall do just as I like with them," answered Peter, "and that means that two or three of my own sort—all smart fellows—none ot your shoddy and size-tubs, 'll have a jolly feed upon them next Satur- day night. As for you, Kit, you see, as I like to do the thing handsome, I don't mind standing you a pound of tripe; it'll be more in your way, you know." "Look here, young snippet, (1-d-dorned thee spend thi 13-h-brass so fast, or tha'll be having t-t-to take thad ring off thi finger and pop id. But awll tell thi wod, aw've bin abeawt this place for nearly twenty year au' aw've alus had a sh-share yet o' these Kessmus comforts. This is fast time as ther's bin onny-b-body in thy shop g-g-greedy enough to want o to hissel ; but ther's two sides to a ladder, soa thad b-b-better look eawt. Tha may grin and screw thad b-b-bit o' yure, but if tha g-geds thi meawth knockt up, tha'll have summut else to f-f-feel at." With this vigorous protest against confiscation and spoliation, Kit at once proceeded to his friends the tapers, to inform them crf this unprecedented determination, and to concert a plan of vengeance against Mr. l'eter as their natural enemy. They were all agreed that he should not go unpunished for thus seeking to deprive them of the annual ' good picking. But how ?—that was the question. One suggested that they should tumble him into an empty flour-sack and roll him across the floor; another that they should take his best coat (for Peter had an old garment to work in) and fill the pockets with sodden size about an hour before he would re- quire it on leaving the mill; but Kit inclined to a gastronomic feat upon rabbit and turkey, if they could only get possession of those coveted dainties. That something should be done was a settled point. They had no fear of a complaint as to their misde- meanour; for, in that case, a knowledge of the cause of the quarrel would necessarily reach the ears of the heads of the firm, and they were known to strongly disapprove of these Christmas presents. On the following day Kit ascertained that Mr. Peter had secured the favours awaiting him at Mr. Turnspit's; and, further, that the said favours—as Mr. Pete' put it—were to be "served up first-class" to Mr. Peter and his friends, along with some "capi- tal.fixings," at six o'clock on Christmas Eve. Mrs. Puncheon, of the Jolly Miller, was going to "do the thing ploper—everything tip-top—fit for the Lord Mayor—and no mistake." Christmas Day this year fell on the Sunday. This was rriday, and the annual stock-taking had, as usu.al, to be completed beforeleaving the works on Christmas Eve. Now it rested with Kit, in a great measure, whether they should have finished early or late on the Saturday. He usually toiled like a slave with a view to expedite matters; bat his first thought, on hearing of the dinner at the Jolly Miller, was to take things from that moment provokingly easy, and thus compel Mr. Peter to be detained at the mill a couple of hours beyond the appointed time, This was all very good on the face of it; but what kept one would detain the other, and making Peter miserable was but a left-handed way, after all, of ensuring Kit's felicity. And, besides, the dinner would be demolished under any circumstances, for he felt assured that Mr. Peter's "friends would, before waiting very long, fall-to and eat, even if Mr. ' Peter should be absent. A vision of the flesh-pots haunted Kit for half the day; his bowels of com- passion yearned for a,close acquaintance with "a leg and a bit oth' breast." Much pondering at length brought him relief. He suddenly struck his thigh with his left hand, and stretching out his right arm after the manner of the first villain in a third-rate melodrama, he exclaimed. "I have it! I have it!
oody " To'
t book

The g-g-game is mine!" Then he hastened, at the first opportunity, to his fellowaconspirators in the taping-room, and bade them be at the Jolly Miller at a quarter past six on the following evening. They must not ask him a single question, or say a word to anyone; only be there at the time, and they should have " torkey and rapput,—fixings an' a, and everything tip-top.' That Kit was in earnest they could plainly see. They were convinced that he did not intend to play any trick upon them, and re- solved, tinder the circumstances, to— Shut their eves and open their mouths. And hopefully trust in Providence. Saturday came, and with it the burden of stock- taking-- to Mr. Peter the task of counting, entering, tad :adding; to Kit the toil of wheeling, lifting, and carrying. They laboured on, those two, hard and patiently; but at four o'clock there was well- nigh two hours' work before them. Mr. Peter was getting impatient, and endeavoured to spur Kit to in- creased exertion. Kit, however, doggedly kept to his old pace, so that it was nearly six o'clock when the last skip of bobbins in the warping-room was weighed and entered. Although altogether unusual for Saturday, the engines were running on this occasion to enable the mechanics to complete sonic new pieces of mach- inery which were to be fit up during the brief stop- page for Christmas. The warping-room was in the third story, and there was, as in the room below, a communication with the yard by a door which was only used when something had to be hoisted into the room,or vice versa, transported from thence to the yard. This door had stood ajar for some time, and Kit now stood within a few feet of it, near an empty skip, with jacket on, as if ready to receive the order to go. "Bolt that door, and then make a bolt of it your- self," said Mr. Peter, as lie struggled into his great coat. " And w-w-wod abeawt this dinner like?—has there to b-be coy?" "Rather I A spiffin' dinner, ray boy, I can tell you; but, as the clown says in the circus, not for you; so clear out, you lubber, and let's be off, or I shall have the whole boiling on me for keeping them waiting." " C-c-come neaw, aw'll just gio thi another ch- chance," said Kit. "has it to b-b-be share an' share alike o reawnd ? Fair doos, tha knows." "None of your cheek, Kit; you booby, what do you want? You should have had the tripe if you hadn't kept me here so long with your snail crawl- ing. Nothing from me, I can tell you—not even a sheep's trotter : and, as for the dinner, I'll be hanged before you shall touch it." " Theigher," said Kit, " tha's just hit it theer, ml t-t-tulip," and without another word he flung open the hoist door, rudely seized Mr. Peter's sacred person, and tumbled him head foremost into the skip. Then he instantly clapped the hoist hooks to each side, pushed on the strap which worked the apparatus, and before Mr. Peter could think what had happened, he was swinging out into the frosty air, and descending rapidly into the mill-yard. His descent was, however, suddenly arrested; Kit had knocked off the driving-strap, and Mr. Peter found himself suspended in mid-air—about three yards from the warping room, at least five yards from terra firma, and a great many miles from the full moon which was looking down on him from the eastern sky. "Well, heaw d-d-does ta like thad ?" said Kit, as soon as he saw that Peter was realising his perilous position in the wicker-work carriage. "Thu s-s-said tha'd 'be hanged,' and it looks summat like it, d-dangling theer in that skip." "None of your chaff, Kit, this is really dangerous; hoist me up at once, I say." "Really, Betty, wod a g-g-gaffer tha'd make! Is there owt as aw c-c-con do for thi? Keen frost air w-'will make thi hungry, aw dar say. Shall aw g-g-ged thi a sooap o' size, and some o' thad sh-sh- shoody as the were talking aba.awt. r+et.siday "Tou shall suffer for this, fellow, as soon as I get at liberty." And Mr. Peter thereupon screamed out at the top of his voice for "Old Richard," the watchman. "Dorn'd be so rash avi thi sh-sh-sheawtin,"said Kit, after listening and laughing for a minute or two: " tha'll happen b-b-brast a blood-vessel, and then we shall want a d-d-doctor. Tha might run f-for a pleeceman while tha'rt making thud noise, and d-d-do th' job gradely." "Come Kit, let me out of this; you've done enough„' pleaded Peter. "0 streight and s-square abeawc thad dinner?' asked Kit. . "Not for you, blockhead! The watchman will be here directly, and then you'll get dinner." " Darn'd thee fret thisel: abeawt th' watchman, yung cony-wig; he's gone to ther Sarah's to his tay, an' aw'm off to m-m-mine; so tha c-c-con skrike thisel gomeless if t'likes." Kit now turned away, and proceeded to close the door, upon which his victim called out— "Look here, man ; you'll never leave me starving here. Hoist me up, and you shall have as much turkey as you like." " Tha really m-meons "Certainly; of course I do." "Then tha mon write and t-t-tell Mrs. Puncheon to let me and th' tapers have thud d-dinner in fost thing. Look eawt ! Ther's stock b-b-book an' a blackhead." And, with this remark, Kit took a book and pencil from the desk and dropped them into the skip. 'Put id in thi own words; tha knows wod aw w-w-wa,nt. Ther's plenty o' moon-leet for a job o' that sort." Seeing the helplessness of his position, and that there was no other alternative, Mr. Peter com- menced to write as well as his half-benumbed fingers would permit him. Having finished the note, he tore the leaf out of the book, and, holding it up, said— • ."Now, Kit, it's all ready.' Hoist me in, and you shall have the note." "Nod so f-fast theer...-nod so fast," said Kit. "Aw mun hi o'th' safe side; a bird i'th' hand's worth two i'th' b-b-bush ; ' soa just fasten th' note on this string, and let's mak sure on't." Suiting the action to _Use word, Kit, holding one end of a few yards of twine, let the other fall into the skip. Peter added a line to the note, and then tied the precious document to the cord, by which it was immediately conveyed into Kit's possession. 'On taking the paper to a light, Kit read as fol- lows : Millbrook Mill, Christmas Eve. "Dear Mrs. Puncheon,—l am unexpectedly de- tained here for a short time. Please to serve up dinner immediately to bearer and those who are with him.—Yours, &c., PETER PENMAN. " P.S. —Tell my friends to wait for me in the bar I will explain matters as soon as I see them.—P. P.' " Theigherl " exclaimed ' Kit, " that'll d-d-do." Then, turning to Peter, he said, "Ta-ta, my torkey- cock, aw'm off to d-d-dinner. It's nod often as aw ged a good b-b-blow-eawt." "But pull me in; be quick. Kit; I shall be frozen." "Then freeze away; ther's b-b-better fooak nor thee had ther nooases pinched afore to day. Awli send s-s-sombry to the' afore morning. Aw'm off neaw for that tripe; sari. t-t-ta-ta." Kit closed the hoist door, leaving Peter literally and metaphorically "out in the cold ;" and then he hurried out of the mill in high spirits at the success of his stratagem. Five minutes' quick walking brought him to the Jolly Miller; and he had barely delis- =red the important missive into the hands of the landlady when his friends the tapers—punctual to a minute—presented themselves at the door. "Here they are," said Kit, as soon as he saw them; and they were at once shown into the dining-room. Mrs. Puncheon was not a little puzzled at these un- expected guests; but she had the note—it was there in "black and white "—so she hastened to tell Mr. Peter's select circle in the bar, who were drinking and smoking as a means of gaining an appetite, that Mr. Peter had been detained at the mill; he would, however, be with them in a few minutes, and explain why he had kept them waiting. This message pro- voked, net unnaturally, 'a 'show of impatience; but it was instantly allayed when, at Mrs Puncheon's suggestion, it was resolved to "have drinks round" at Mr. Peter's expense. But how fared the company in the other room? Ah, how should four healthy hungry men fare with a young turkey done to a turn; two rabbit pies, with a crust which defied criticism; mincemeat which would have glacTdened the heart of an epicure : and tempting tarts and jellies altogether "too numerous to mention,".to summarise the catalogue in orthodox catalogue style,—how should they fare, those four bard-working men, who had been looking forward for weeks at the prospects a a dinner not half so good as the one before them? Truly— Kingi may be blest, but they were glorious— O'er a' the ills o' life victorious. Dinner nearly over, Kit seemed suddenly to re- member that he ought to have informed Mr. Peter's choice friends to call upon him at the mill if he was not with them ha a very short time. "They would have to get in by the boiler-house gate," he said, "for the watch-house was closed." Mrs. Puncheon willingly conveyed this second message; and away went these representatives of fopdom to Millbrook, where they found the pet of their party crouched in the dangling skip, cold as

an icicle, but hot-tempared as an Irishman, and keeping pace with the barking watch-dog with his hitherto fruitless cries for assistance. His story was soon told, and they were all agreed that, as most of the edibles would by that time have disappeared, it would be the least mortifying to leave Kit and his friends in undisturbed posses- sion of the good things at the Jolly Miller, and trust to their kindly natures in refraining from making it known how severely the biter had been bitten. The joke, however, was too good to be lost. It was soon noised through Millbrook Mill, and Mr. Peter heard so much of it that he found it desirable ere long to taken situation elsewhere. Kit remained at the mill for many, many years. His claim to a share of the perquisites was never afterwards disputed; for as often as the time came round for the annual feast at the Jolly Miller, he was to be found at his post, hungry as ever, and with stumbling tongue that knew no rest until he had again told the story of his stratagem for securing his Christmas comforts.

CHRISTMAS AND OTHER BOOKS. ; SECOND NOTICE. "Noah's Ark is a tale of the Norfolk Broads by Harley Dale, author of "The Village Blacksmith,' "Fair Kathleen," &c., and it is published by Messrs. F. Warne and Cu. It cannot be said of this novel that it is strong in the matter of plot, the main incidents turning to the somewhat threadbare supposition of the change of children in the nurs- ing. The pictures of Norfolk life are, however, exceedingly well drawn, the local colouring being in many cases extremely striking. The various char- acters are firmly portrayed, that of "Old Noah" being particularly fine. He is a sturdy type of English manhood in the lower ranks of life; an aristocrat, so to speak,of his own class, without any trace of what we may call class distinction. The illustrations are by Paul Hardy. They are cleverly done and are in complete harmony with the text. "heart of Gold," published by the same firm, is from the pen of L. T. Meade, author of "Scamp and I," "Daddy's Boy" &c. This is a story of an altogether superior kind. The various personages are sharply , defined. The plot is made to evolve itself naturally out of opposite extremes of character which are brought, as in life, incidentally together. A contrast in the charac- ter and career of two sisters is very marked, and it is worked out with a most skilful hand. Every chapter contains something interesting, and the reader who I commences the story will be constrained to read it through. It is illustrated in a capital style by Messrs. 113. Partridge and S. Thorn. "Heart of Gold," like "Noah's Ark" is well bound and well printed, and pub- lished at 3s. 6d. " Barker's Facts and Figures," published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co., is an exceedingly useful hand-book, edited by Mr. T. P. Whittaker. It contains a large and reliable amount of information relating to commerce, Government, agriculture, population,education,religion, railways, &c., with some account of the general condi- tion of various nations and peoples. It should be added that the type is good, and that the matter is admirably arranged for the purposes of ready reference. " Rex Raynor, artist," is a story of " sowing and reaping," by the Rev. S. K. Hocking, the well-known author of " Herr Benny," &c. This story is sure to have a large number of readers, Mr. Hocking being well- known and much admired as a writer who always pre- serves an elevating tone, and has a moral purpose in view in everything he undertakes. The tale is one which illustrates a great blunder, or perhaps we should say crime, and what became of it in the course of a life tune. The illustrations are not numerous, but they are of a superior kind. The price of the book is 2s. 6d., and it is published by Messrs. Warne and Co. " Women painters of the Victorian Era," edited with an introduction and notes by Mrs. Sharp, is tho title of the latest issue of the " Canterbury Poets" series, pub- .' to
forth" 1

have biought the women poets of th, preserit together in a shillig volume; and Mrs. Sharp must be congratulated nix): he admirable way in which she has done her work. We suspect that many readers who are fAmilar with sundry well-known songs and poems will be surprised to find that they have been written by women. It is a matterof course to say that the most noted women of the Victorian Era are represented in the

volume—such as Harriett Martineau, 'Sara Cole-ridge, Lady Duffarin, Mrs. Carlyle, Mrs. Browning, Eliza Cook, Dora Greenall, G. Elliot, and Jean Ingalow, &c., &c. It will much surprise us if the book has not, as it deserves

to have, anexiraordinary sale. The Christmas number of tho "Graphic " a wonderful shilling's worth. The presentationis, as usual, plate is a reproduction in the highest form of chromo-lithography of the picture by Sir Frederick Leighton, F.R.A.,entitled , "Desdemona." The coloured illustrations Of the number proper include a story without words--" A proposal of marriage," "The fox o'one tree hill," " Eddie's buffer trap," "Naval Manoeuvres -go-round on the ice." "A winning hazard,, ~A merry," &c. mr, • , Thomas Hardy writes the principal story under the tit'e " A group of noble dames."

The principal presentation plate with the Christmas number of the "Illustrated London News," is " Little Jack Homer," after the original painting by Jan Van Beers. It is a beautiful picture of a beautiful boy; and, when framed, will be an adornment for any home. Two smaller chromo plates bear the title of " Swing " and "Idle moments." The other illustrations are in black and white, and they are all powerfully executed. The main story "The only shadow," is the conjoint produc- tion of Christie Murray and Henry Herman; and there is, besides, a contribution by that rising author Rudyard Kipling. " Truths "Christmas number is in verse as heretofore, and is celebrated with several coloured and numerous other plates. All the " urns" are hit off, and by means of" Hypnotism" "Truth "interviews everybody who is anybody, and there is of course some fine fun. The satire is pungent but good humoured, and cannot but have a wholesome effect. The number is a good shillings- worth. • "The Strand Magazine" makes its first appearance in December; and, as a sixpenny publication, it is likely to be in great demand. The illustrations are numerous, and, considering the price, are excellent. One capital feature is a series of portraits of eminent persons, the idea being to give the appearance of these people at different stages of their lives from youth upwards. Some of the short stories are translations from eminent foreign authors, but they are not likely to be less welcome on that account. Along with the first number, there is a presentation plate of the picture known as "Tit-Bits," from an original painting by Madame Amyot. " Weldon's Ladies Journal "is published at sixpence as a Christmas number. Besides coloured and other plates , of fashion and a paper pattern, we have two presentation ; plates, one " The wrong move" the other "In mischief ' again," both from original oil paintings in the possession of the publishers. The publishers of " Cope's Tobacco Plant," Liverpool, have issued three of their excellent "Smoke room book- lets." One is Charles Lamb in pipes full ;" another , deals with " Carlyle," both being accompanied with portraits ; and the third is" The smoker's garland." "The Magic Calendar" is a series of cleverly designed cards published by Messrs. M. Ward and Co. Ltd.' the object of which is tell a person's birthday, wedding day, or the date of any other event in the year. The cards are calculated to provide plenty of innocent fun at the Christmas party. We have also to hand in the way of Christmas num- bers, "Fun Almanack " twopence, and "Fun's Merry Moments," one penny, both excellent alike in text and illustration ; " Answers," price twopence, with a pre- sentation chromo-lithograph and a number of funny sketches ; also " Ally Sloper's Christmas Holidays." MESSRS. RAPHAEL TUCK AND SONS BOOKLETS AND CHRISTDIAS CARDS.

Variety is charming, but it is also a little bewildering when it comes in the shape of such a flood of things novel and beautiful as issues from the premises of Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons. They lead the way in fine-art Christmas cards and booklets. The present season's goods show that they are still to the front and likely to be to the front. To the ordinary observer it seems, every year, as if ingenuity has exhausted itself in designing fresh novelties ; but art knows no limit in these matters, and Messrs. Tuck and Sons evidently know n 3 limit in their commission to artists. Such a unique production as Herriek's poem "Let's go a-Maying," as illustrated by Bessie Nicol, is something to be admired not merely at Christmas but all the year round. The illustration to the suterb line—" The light hangs on the dewlocks of the night "is equal to the occasion, for it too, is superb. "Little Ah Sid" is one of the most comical things in literature, and it is most comically, and yet most artisti- cally illustrated by Messrs. Wilde, Ostrander, and T. R. Kennedy. It begins : Little Ah Sid Was a Christian kid • And a 'cute little cus you'd declare ; With eyes full of fun , And a nose that begun Right up in the roots of his hair. ' "Tie song of the shirt" is preiented with a cover that takes the shape of a huge bobbin of thread, and it is likely • to be in special demand in its new setting of clever illus- tration by J. W. Grey. Amongst other dainty " shaped " booklets we have in bucket shape the famous poem of the " Bucket." prettily illustrated by Annie and Bessie Simpson ; " Lilies," a series of beauifully illustrated poems by Edith P. Snowdon; And "A Basket of Mis- chief" with clever verse and illustrations for the little ones. ",Nature's Treasures " by H. Marion Burnside seems too dainty to be handled, with its wealth of illus- trations by L. Pryce, I. S. Walker. "Singing through the year,' and that purely Christmas poem" Evermore," are equally good in their way. • The " Gem Art Calenders " will be welcomed, for they will find a place on the wall or mantelpiece as alike use- ful and ornamental. The "porcelain studies " show a distinct advance in this class of art. One of the most charming is a scene admirably coloured, and set in a

"Then do so. When he is dead two hundred ducats are yours." "Then he dies." " Goodl—And now there is one more. This gun maker must be got out of the way." "Ah," muttered Savotano, looking up incredul- ously. "Do you mean so?" "Most assuredly I do." "But why him?" "Do you fear to undertake the work ?" 1 "Not at all, my lord; I only wished know why he was wanted away." "The reason is simple. I must marry wih Rosa- lind Valdai. Her property is worth the whole of Drotzen twice told—over two million of ducats." "So much ?" uttered the priest, opening his eyes with greedy wonder. " Yes ; it is one of the finest estates in Moscow, and it pays her now a yearly income of a hundred thousand ducats. She does not know it—Ha, ha. ha—"

"Ha, ha, ha," laughed the priest in concert. "She don't, eh ?" "No—she knows nothing about it. But I must secure this; and in order to do it I must marry her; and—if I would be sure of that; this accursed gun- maker must be out of the way." "But what is he to her ? " "She loves him." "And is not your authority—" " Hold, Savotano. I'll explain to yon in a few words. I'm afraid the Emperor has taken a fancy to this youngster, and if he has he may be appealed to in this case. The girl will take marriage hard. I shall have to hire you to perform the ceremony. "Which I should be pleased to do," returned the priest, with a coarse smile. "You shall have the opportunity. But first we must have the young Nevel taken care of." " I think I can manage that, my lord." "And how will you do it ? " "I suppose you don't want him put where he can get off and come back here." "No. Finish him while you are about it !" " I will." "But mind: it must be done so that in no pos- sible way suspicion can fall upon me. You must contrive some way so that suspicion shall be led at once to some apparent point, and there baffled." " Leave me alone for that, my lord. I can call help if I want it." Are there not places in the city where a body' can be hidden ?—where they may be disposed of and never be found ? " asked the duke, as the thought came to his mind. Never mind," returned the other, with a confi- dent nod of the head. "If I meddle with the matter it shall be well done.', "Very well. I'll trust it to you." For a few moments after this there was a dead silence, during which only the moaning of the wind could be heard. But at length the duke started up, and with sudden energy he said: " Ah, Savotano, there is one thing I came nigh forgetting. You have heard of this strange monk— Valdimir his name is." "Aye—and I have seen him too. "You mean that huge lump of human fat ?” "Yes. And now tell me who and what he M- lle was at the duel ; and I know he has been here to my house. Who is he ? " " You've secured me there, my lord, for I can tell you no more about him than I can about the man in the moon. In short no one seems to know him,. save that he is a monk, of some Roman order, and named Valdimir. He has been here only a few months, as near as I can find out. And yet I think I know what his business is : or, at least, why he's I here." .
" Ah—you suspect." "4,4"--141. 4 • w:in " Yes—and if my suspicions be coirect we could have him taken care of at any moment." "Explain." _ _

EXPORTS. With regard to the iffect of the lil'Hinley Tariff on English interests, the subjoined are the conclusions of a memorandum to the Board of Trade. This tariff subjects an import trade into the United States of nearly £80,000,000, now bearing a burden of £32,000,000, or 41 percent., to a burden of £41,000,000, or 52 per cent. But according to the memorandum the alarm with which the Wliinley Tariff, as regards its effect on the general trade of the world, and the trade between Eng- land and the United States in particular, has been viewed, cannot but be considered as exaggerated. It will devert and disturb tradepre tanto, but it effects only a part of the United States foreign trade, and a still smaller part indeed of their total trade, while many of the increased duties, for various reasons, are either not productive in effect, or cannot effect the protection aims] at.

div.head: " WRECK " OS THE WEINER.
div.p: A " WRECK " OS THE WEINER.

Owing to the suspension of river traffic on Sunday, the Weaver became sheeted with ice, which thickened considerably towards Monday. At five o'clock that morning several steamers were employed in ploughing through the heavy mass, in order to render navigation possible, and by eight or nine o'clock the stream had been almost made open. About half-past nine the small towing steamer Nymph was running at a good speed from the Navigation Works to the Town Bridge, at which spot the engineer discovered that a sharp piece of ice had penetrated her side, through which the water rapidly Poured. Full steam being put on, the vessel was quickly run under the bridge into a small creek, where the crew succeeded in springing on to the river bank. They were none too soon, for within five minntes the little craft sank, as far as the ropes would allow, the wat•ermen hav- ing managed to moor her. The " wreck " was raised in the course of the day, the damage sustained being com- paratively slight.

div.head: WAGES IN THE COTTON TRADE.
div.p: WAGES IN THE COTTON TRADE.
AN ADVANCE GRANTED.

-- A meeting of Master Bolton Cotton Spinners' Associa- tion was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Victoria Hotel, Manchester, to consider the position of affairs with re- gard to the wages question. The Operative Cotton Spinners' Association tendered & month's notice for an advance equivalent to 5 per cent. This notice expires, according to the making-up days. this week. Shnulta- neously with the operatives' claim, the card and blowing room hands tendered notices for an advance of 10 per cent, for males and 5 per cent, for females. The ques- tion for the masters to consider was whether they would permit the stoppage of their mills for a week rather than concede the demand. After about an hour's delibera- tion it was announced that the masters had granted the rnen'sdemands in full. There will, therefore, be no strike and the hands who intended to leave' work will remain at their posts. The advance comes into operation at once,

div.head: BASSETLA.W ELECTION.
div.p: THE BASSETLA.W ELECTION.
RESULT OF THE POLL,

The result of the polling in the Bassetlaw Division of Nntts, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. William I3eckett, was declared on Tuesday as follows : Sir Frederick Milner (C) Hight Bon. J. W. Mellor (L)

Majority .. 728 In 1886 the constituency was not contested, but in 1835 the Conservative majority was 295. The figures for that and the present election were : 1885 1890 Conservative 4,367 ... 4,381... inc. 14 Liberal

Majority... 293 728 Whereas 8,439 voters went to the poll in 1885, only 8 044 did so on Monday. A special correspondent at Retford,writing on Tuesday night, says :—The little town of Retford this morning,as the time drew on for the declaration of the poll, hardly looked equal to the occasion. The crowd was much smaller than might have been expected. This was no doubt due in a great measure to the same cause that kept down the polling the day before to an unexpectedly low figure. The weather was very severe, and the roads 48 sheets of glass. At nine o'clock the counting com- menced. and just before eleven the result was declared by the High Sheriff of Nottingham from the Town Hall balcony. There were four or five hundred people down below, and the Town Hall windows were thronged. The verifying of the papers overnight had enabled the party leaders to adticipate roughly the position of affairs, but the actual figures seems to have come as something as a EllrPrise to both parties. It need tigirdly be said that the Conservatives received the announcement in the most boisterous delight, while a good many of the rougher portion of the voters on the other side were un- able to conceal their disappointment. Sir Frederick Milner's speech was inaudible, and Mr. Mellor's was very brief. He thanked them for the hearty kindness they had shown to him during his stay among them, and urged upon them the necessity of organisation.

div.head: HOME RULE CRISIS.
div.p: HOME RULE CRISIS.

- FACTION FIGHTS IN THE KILIKENNNY CONTEST. , At Kilkenny, on Saturday, the greatest uncertainty . prevailed as, to Mr. Parnell's movements. He had in- tended to leave forWaterford and Limerick on Saturday night, but after, several contrary announcements the journey was finally abandoned. Addressing a meeting on Saturday afternoon in support of Mr. Vincent Scully's condidature, Mr. Parnell, who spoke from the windows of the Victoria Hotel, made a fierce attack on Sir John ,Popellennessy, whose political record, would not bear inspection. He had belonged to every party but the Irish party, and was only fit to lead renegades. Sir John Pope Hennessy, Mr. Healy, Mr. Michael Davitt, and Dr. Tanner visited several county districts of the constitu- ency on Saturday, and delivered addresses. The princi- pal meeting was at Castlecomer, a busy mining centre, where they had a magnificant reception. Mr. Parnell also addressed meetings in North Kilkenny, on Sunday, in support of the candidature of Mr. Vincent Scully. In these speeches he repeated his attacks on Sir John Pope Hennessy and that candidate's supporters, and declared Pie issue nefore the constituency was whether they would choose their own leader and Parliamentary repre- sentatives,or be dictated to by Englishmen and renegades. The man who imprisoned him in 1882, but failed to break his spirit, or to break the spirit of Ireland by coer- cion, now sought to attack the independence of her members in another fashion, but Ireland would foil him. An anti-Parnellite meeting was held at Tipperary on Sunday afternoon, but the proceedings were so noisy and tumultuous, and at times so threatening, that little or nothing of the speeches made by Mr. Condon, M.P., Mr. P. J. O'Brien, M.P., and Father Humphreys could be heard except by those close to the platform. Though some stones were thrown and sticks were flourished menacingly, so far as could be ascertained, no one pre- sent was seriously injured. ' MONDAY. Mr. Vincent Scully and Sir J. Pope Hennessy were on Monday nominated for Kilkenny, as Parntllite and anti- Parnellite candidates respectively. There was no Con- servative nomination. An objection of a trivial charac- ter was raised by Mr. Scully to the validity of Sir J. Pope Hennessy's nomination, but the objection was not pressed. The anti-Parnellites held a meetihg at Rath- downey, where they met Mr. Parnell, who had been briefly addressing a meeting in the same place' but no serious conflict occurred. Dr. Tanner said that he and his colleagues had been called "gutter sparrows" by Mr. Parnell, but at any rate they declined to whitewash his blasted character. Mr. Patrick O'Brien, M.P., and Mr. O'Brien Dalton, M.P., who are now in gaol, hays intimated their determination to stand by Mr. Parnell. Mr. Parnell had promised to speak on Monday night at Kilmanagh, but he suddenly left the train at Bally- ragget.

TUESDAY. Both Parnellites and Anti-Parnellites held meetings on Tuesday, at Ballinakill, and great excitement prevailed in the district. Both parties addressed their audiences at the same time, and a severe fight took place, blackthorn being freely used. Mr. Devitt, after accusing the other side of promoting the disorder, jumped off his car and pushed his way amongst the contestants, he was several times struck, and freely returned the blows with a stout stick. On returning to his car after the fight, Mr. Davitt, whose hat was in ribbons, said that he and his followers bad beaten the other side, and they would beat them again. Mr. Devitt and other Anti-Parnellites then drove on to Castlecomer, and on Mr. Parnell and his party ap- pearing, some of the blackthorn incidents of the BsHine- kill meeting were repeated. Mr. Parnell was quite un- able to make his voice heard in the uproar. His party were covered with mud, and he was struck in the face with a bag of lime and temporarily blinded, necessitating an hour's stay at a cottage in order to receive surgical treatment.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Mr. Parnell suffered considerably on Wednesday from the effects of the lime-throwing on the previous evening, and his eyes being completely bandaged up, he was un- able to leave the house. Dr. Tanner, M.P., Mr. Kenny- M.P. , Mr. Deasy, M.P., and Mr. Davitt addressed a meet- ing of anti-Parnellites at Freshford. Mr. Davitt gave a description of the fight at Ballinakill and alleged that the disturbance was caused by Mr. Parnell ordering hisbrake to be dragged int,i close quarters with the opposition meeting. Dr. Tanner expressed the indignation which he felt at seeing Mr. Davitt struck, and said that in con- sequence of this he the doctor) hit out right and left. He also alleged that. the Parnellites spat in the faces of the anti-Parnellite priests. Meetings were also held in support of Mr. Vincent Scully, the Parnellite candidate. A manifesto issued by the Irish Presbyterian General Assembly deplores the immorality which has all along characterised the National movement. According to an Armagh correspondent a vacancy is about to occur in the representation of Mid-Armagh, owing to the resignation of Sir James Porter Corry, on account of ill-health. The Unionists have adopted Mr. Dunbar Barton, Q.C.,as their candidate. The leaders of the anti -Parnellite section of the Irish Parliamentary party had an opportunity of testing their position in the city of Cork on Wednesday. Mr. Justin M'Carthy, M.P., and Mr. Sexton, M.P., Who,. on the previous night, were the objects on their arrival of a demonstration more noisy than friendly, addressed a meeting in the Assembly-room, a spacious building,which was crowded. Both the hon. gentlemen named addressed the gathering onthe question of the hour, and with both the audience proved itself to be thoroughly in sympathy. The meeting,which was harmonious throughout, passed resolutions approving the action of Mr. WCarthy and his colleagues in the majority with reference to the leadership question, and denouncing the selfish and un- patriotic conduct of Mr. Parnell.
lead,

THURSDAY. The campaign in North Kilkenny was vigorously pro- secuted by the leading speakers on both sides on Thurs- day. Contrary to the advice of his doctors, and with one of his eyes still bandaged, Mr. Parnell drove to meetings at Goresbridge and Gowran, where he deli- vered short speeches, and was well re.ceived. On the other side, Mr. Davitt and Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P., made an excursion to Urlingford, in their opponents' country, and some of the inhabitants showed the view they took of the visit by putting up their shutters. SCENE IN THE KILKENNY COUNCIL.

An extraordinary scene occured in the Kilkenny Town Council on Thursday, consequent on an attempt to move a resolution of confidence in the Anti-Parnellite party. Two members, Alderman Rowan and Captain O'Leary, were only prevented from coming to blows by the inter- position of their colleagues, and after the anti-Parnellites had left, a resolution of confidence in Mr. Parnell was carried.
ROMAN CATHOLIC OPINION,

At the last mass on Sunday a circular from Bishop Cloyne, addressed to his clergy, was read, stating that in consequence of the deplorable state of things produced by Mr. Parnell's unprincipled and unpatriotic action in degrading the struggle for freedom, it was of the utmost importance to organize branches of the National League throughout the diocese, and urging the necessity for convening meetings of the branches of the National League in the diocese to explain the necessity that ex- ists for withdrawing themselves from the control of the central league in Dublin. At Westport, on Sunday, ' statements were delivered in the Roman Catholic Churches denouncing the policy pursued by Mr. Par- nell. "UNITED IRELAND "AND A NEW PAPER. _

In the Dublin Vice-Chancellor's Court on TueAday an application was made on behalf of the Irish National Newspaper and Publishing Company for an Injunction t) restrain Mr. Bodkin and others from publishing or selling any newspaper under the name of " United Ire- land.' Pending the hearing of the action, defendant's council asked for an adjournment. but would not under- take not to publish the paper meanwhile. The Vice- Chancellor thereupon said he had no alternative but to ' grant an injunction, which would issue forthwith. The newspaper published in Dublin by the anti- Parnellite party appeared on Wednesday under the title "Insuppressible—W. O'Brien's Paper." It attributes the result of the Bassetlaw election solely to the deplor- able effect of Mr. Parnell's proceedings. The prospectus lof the limited company which is to issue a new Irish Nationalist daily paper is being circulated. Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., is chairman of directors and editor in thief. The capital of the Company is to be £BO,OOO.

div.head: MIL CHAMBERLAIN'S VIEWS.
div.p: MIL CHAMBERLAIN'S VIEWS.

. _ Speaking at a private meeting of the Liberal Unionist Association at Birmingham on Tuesday night, Mr. T. Chamberlain, M.P., said recent events had removed Howie Rule from the region of practical politics. Lately he had been the recipient of A rather curious corres- pondence. He had heard from many of his former Liberal friends, and they said there was no longer any reason why the Liberal party should not be re-united. But one reason for not accenting this invitation was that Mr. Gladstone still placed Home Rule in the fore- front of political reform. Besides, it was impossible for them to have any dealings with the men who had divorced politics from morality. He thought it pro- bable that out of the recent crisis there might arise a truly national party, a party of progress in the best sense. It was decided at the meeting to form a joint Unionist Committee for the discussion of questions affecting the interests of the Conservative-Unionist Party.

-- Mr. V. B. Dillon, solicitor for the defence in the Tip- perary assault casesonet with a serious accident on Mon- day night, owing to the breakage of a water jug. His leg was badly cut, and he will not be able to leave his room for some days. Mr. John Morley, who arrived in D üblin on Monday, has been telegraphed to. On the judge taking his seat on the Bench, Mr. Adams, Q.C., applied for an adjournment on behalf of the defendants, on the grounds of Mr. Dillon's illness.—Mr. Carson, Q.C., who appeared for the Crown, pointed out the inconvenieace which an adjournment would cause, some of his wit- nesses having to come from England, but left the ques- tion entirely in his lordship's hands. His Lordship sug- getted an :adjournment until next Assizes. This was assented to.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1890. . . . THE TIPPERARY ASSAULT CASES. MURDER IN A CAB AT . LIITERPOOL. Shortly after eight on Wednesday evening, a fatal stabbing outrage occurred in a cab in Liverpool. the vic- tim being a young woman about 24 years of age, and who is now lying dead at the Royal Infirmary. liler name is Margaret Cowie, or Stewart, and she has been living since Thursday week with a man giving the name of Arthur ?infold, at 28, Lambert-street. Pinfold is about 30 years of age, and is said to be employed by a railway company in Liverpool. The woman is stated to have come to Liverpool from Lanark, in Scotland, her father being an hotel proprietor in that place. The man and the woman were in Ranelagh-st. on Wed- nesday evening shortly before eight o'clock, the former being under the influence of drink. They went to the Ranelagh-st. cabstand and engaged a cab Pinfold requested the cabman to drive them to 28, Lambert-et., and they both entered the cab together, Magee, the cabman, shutting the door. On the , way the driver did not notice anything unusual, or that any outcry was made; but when the vehicle arrived at , Lambert-st., on the cabman opening the door, Pinfcld, who made no attempt to get out of the cab, said, "1 have stabbed this woman,cabby. You can go for a police- man, if you like." The cabman replied, "Is it right P" and Pinfold said, "Look," pointing to the woman who was unconscious and covered with blood. Pinfold ;Aided, "lain not going away." The door was immediately closed by the cabman, who called two women to look afterhis cab while he went for a policeman. Two officers at once proceeded to the spot, and found that the woman had been dreadfully stabbed about the body. Police- , constable 668 immediately arrested Pinfold, and took him to the Detective Office, Dale-st., while Police-constable I 31, had the woman taken to the Royal Infirmary in a , cab. She was attended to by Dr. Gould and Dr. feare. who found that she had received six stabs of a serious• nature on the left breast and side. Three of the wounds were superficial, but three others penetrated the left breast and lungs. Her clothes were saturatued with blood. She was unconscious and died shortly after ad- mission. On the way to the Detective Office, Pinfold said "II did it. She asked me to do it." In the Detective Office he said, " I hope she is dead." The police found on the prisoner a large two-bladed clasp knife the longer and larger blade being about four inches long. This blade had apparently been used to inflict the injuries on the woman, as it was covered with blood. The prisoner's hands and part of his clothes were also covered with blood, and when arrested he took matters quite coolly, although he was evidently under the influence of drink. , The deceased, who was an unfortunate, was respectably dressed, and had been previously living in a house in the same street for about five weeks. The prisoner was subsequently charged at the Detee.. two Office with causing the death of the deceased. He said nothing in answer to the charge, but appeared te feel his position very keenly, as he shed a few tears. 138 Informed Mr. Boyce, the well-known Liverpool detective, that he was unmarried, and that he had no father nor mother living, and that he earned his living as a grocer's porter. He states that he was bornin Hertford, and was thirty-one years of age. The sum of is. 4d. was found in his pocket, but no papers. At Liverpool, on Thursday, Arthur Pinfold, grocer's porter, was remanded on a charge of murdering Margaret Stewart, alias Cowie, by stabbing her in a cab on Wed- nesday night.

THE STANLEY-BARTTELOT CON- TROVERSY, Mr. Stanley has been shown a cable report of the meeting of the Aborgines' Protection Society, held in London last week, at which Sir Robert Fowler, M.P., is alleged to have challenged Mr. Stanley to bring an action for libel, by means of which there might be a full expo- sure of the African scandal,and of those scenes connected , with the rear guard which were still untold. Mr. Stanley carefully read the despatch, and said that he did not know much about these alleged hidden scenes. What he knew of the rear guard he had learned only from the officers, and that had all been published. He added :—" The scenes among the followers of 'Pippo° Tib I don't know much about. I was told that some of them caused a great deal of trouble by ill-treating African women. I was told that some of Major Barttelot's officers made vic- tims of the African Women, and that there had been wild scenes and riotous revelling after the native fas- hion." . .

Mr. Stanley, discussing Sir R. Fowler's challenge, said Sir Richard was a warm personal friend of Sir W. bartte- lot. "If they want a trial why do they not appoint or select twelve gentlemen to be a court or commission, and let them examine all the witnesses? Thus all the facts might be brought out. I should like it very much."
