ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
THE VICAR'S FAREWELL SERMON.

The Rev. S. Wilkinson, who has obtained prefer- ment at Timperley, preached his farewell sermon in St. Pees Church on:Sunday evening to a very large congregation. Appropriate hymns were sung. The Vicar selected for his text the words "The Lord is niy Shepherd; I shall not want ;" and after an exposition of the passage he said :—I cannot help feeling to-day what a pleasure it is that, notwith- standing all the faults and failings of the under shepherd, that we have a great Shepherd to guide us and make up for our deficiences and mistakes. It is just 18 years since I first came to this parish as your clergymen, and in re- viewing that period one cannot help having very mixed feelings. I feel that I have made many mistakes, that I have omitted many opportunities for doing good, and that I have not been as zealous and as earnest in my Master's cause as I ought to have been. Therefore, on an occasion like the present, when one thinks of the errors and mistakes of the past, one cannot help feeling very humble, and praying to God that all of them might be forgiven. I have to thank the people of St. Paul's parish and congregation for many acts of kindness to my dear wife and myself. I have to thank them for the way in which they have stood by me on so many occa- sions, and for the ready help which has been given to me in so many of our great parochial works. As I look round the church, which has been greatly improved during the past 18 years, I cannot help feeling thankful for Use work of restoration; for the church at the other end of the parish; and for the largely increased day and Sunday school accommodation. Then there is our Mission Church in Hoyle-st. I have to thank all in the parish most sincerely for having laboured so faithfully and so earnestly, both as officers of the church, and as Sunday school teachers, and as members of the choir, for the labour of love which has been shown to the church. Indeed, words cannot express my gratitude. I cannot tell you how sincerely and truly I love you all: but I thank you and love you from the bottom of my heart. I am not going to say" Good-bye" to you, because I am not going far away from Warrington,: and I hope your coming vicar will often ask me to occupy the pulpit at St. Paul's. We are only going to a neighbouring village in Cheshire, and it will give my dear wife and myself the greatest possible pleasure when you come to Timperley to see us at the Vicarage. I sincerely hope that the con- nection which has existed so long between us and War- rington will not be severed, but continued to our dying day. I hope you will give the same warm support to my successor that you have given to me, and that you will all stick to the church, to your clergyman, and to your work. Let us pray that the work in St. Paul's parish, and in the parish of Timperley may, be successful in the highest sense of the word, and that it may be the means of leading souls to Christ. In conclusion, let me reneat the words I used in my text 18 years ago, when 4 first came among you—" Brethren pray for Us. ' The service was brought to a cohclusion, by the sing- ing of the Vicar's favourite hymn, "Through the night of doubt and sorrow.". HANDSOME PRESENTATIONS TO MR. WILKINSON. On Wednesday evening there was a large gathering in St. Paul's Girls' Schoolroom to witness several presentations to the Rev. S. and Mrs. IVilkinson before their departure from Warrington for Timperley. The presents included a purse containing the large sum of £257, an address handsomely bound and illuminated, a writing secretaire, and a travelling bag and dressing case. Alderman Sutton was elected to preside, and amongst those present besides Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson, were the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. T. Morris, D. Jones, D. W. Finney, J. Smethurst, Dr. White, J. He_sketh, W. Richardson C. Ashurst, A. J. Jolley, &c. _ , . .

The Ciunzaraw read a letter from the Hon.-Elizabeth Wilson-Patten in which she expressed regret on behalf of Lord Winmarleigh that his present state of health would not allow of his attending the meeting. Letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. J. C. Parr, the Rector of Warrington, and the Rev. G. D. Wray were also read. He added that Mr. Jeans had also asked him to apologise for not being able to attend. Address- ing Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson, the chairman said they had asked them there that night in order to bid them farewell before they left Warrington. He would not say that was a final farewell, for they all hoped to have the pleasure of Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson's com- pany on very many occasions in the future. (Hear, hear.) They grieved to lose Mr. Wilkinson's welcome companionship and the benefit of his spiritual advice, but they rejoiced that he was going, as they hoped, to a more prosperous appointment, and they hoped that both of them, especially Mrs. Wilkinson, who had not been so very well of late, would have health and strength to fulfil those charitable duties which their hearts were fixed upon. They could not forget the many valuable services rendered to that parish during the 18 years Mr. Wilkinson was vicar. Whea he came to Warrington, he found the church of St. Paul's a different edifice to what it was now. At that time, too, in St. Ilarnabas' parish they had to worship in an old barn, but, through Mr. Wilkinson's instrumentality the very handsome and substantial building of St. Barnabas' Church had been erected at a very considerable cost. Mr. Wilkinson had also been the means of erecting in St. Paul's parish All Saints Mission, which was another comfortable building in which service was held for the poor people residing in that district. The Chairman also referred to the now prosperous conditicn of the day and Sunday schools, and concluded by saying that he considered they were very much indebted to Mr. Wilkinson for the benefits he had conferred, not only on the pal ish of St. Paul's, but also upon the whole community, (Applause.) Mr. D. JONES then read the address, which was to be presented to Mr. Wilkinson, and which was as follows: "To the Rev. S. Wilkinson, M.A., Vicar of St. Paul's Church, Warrington, and Mrs. Wilkinson. Dear Mr.and Mrs. Wilkinson,—We the wardens, sidosinen, lay repre- sentatives, and members of St Paul's Church, together with your numerous other friends whose names are here appended, desire to express our sincere and heartfelt re- gret at the loss we are about to sustain in your retire- ment from this parish, and removal from Warrington. During the 18 years you have laboured amongst us in this large and thickly-populated district, you have been unremitting in your conscientious endeavours to promote the moral, spiritual, and material welfare of your par- ishioners. It is particularly gratifying to us to know that your kindly dispositions and charitable con- duct on all occasions have not only won the affection and regard of your own congregation and residents in the district, but also gained the esteem of all classes of the community, and especially of the poor who will greatly miss your ministrations and valuable help. In bespeaking your kind acceptance of this address, and the purse of gold to which all have sus- cubed, as some slight acknowledgement of our warm recognition ot your united valuable services for so many years in connection with St. Paul's, it is most gratifying for you to be able to reflect that you leave a Church School and other affiliated organisations in a very har- monious and excellent condition, and that you take our cordial good wishes for your future prosperity and happi- ness. We fervently hope that your new parishioners at Timperly may long enjoy the benefit of your pastoral care." The address was signed by T. Suttcn (vicar's warden), D. Jones (people's warden), and the fcllowing sidesmen : T. Morris, C. Ashurst, J. Smethurst, W. Law- less, J. Adams, J. Heyes, J. Lawless, W. Chantry, D. W. Finney, and W. Richardson. The names of the sub- scribers was also appended to the address. The CHAIRMAN then handed to Mr. Wilkinson the purse of gold which, he said, contained 257 sovereigns. Mr. T. Morris, Mr. D. W. Finney, and Mr. James Smethurst also spoke and testified to the valuable ser- vices rendered by Mr. and Mrs. Wilkinson.

_ The Rev. S. WILKINSON, who met with a very cordial reception, expressed the thanks of Mrs. Wilkinson and himself for the noble gifts that had been made to them. He referred to his labours in the parish during the last 18 years, and to the loyal help that he had always received from thoseoonnected with St. Paul's Church. He could say that since the time he first came amongst them, he had never had one moment's against any one in the parish, and he had never received anything but kindness and courtesy. He could also say that although he was a Conservative and a Churchman, he had always been able to shake hands with Radicals ,of Warrington. and to have a friendly feeling towards I the Dissenters of the town. (Applause.) He referred to I the resolution 'With regard to his departure that had been passed by the Temperance Federation, and said he was glad to add that, while never budging from his pirn- ciples and never forgetting that he was a Church of England clergyman, at the same time he had always been able to hold out the right hand of fellowship to everyone who thought differently to himself. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. A. J. Jolley then presented Mr. Wilkinson with the travelling bag and dressing case and writing secret- aim on behalf of the members of St. Paul's Mutual Imyrovement Society and the teachers of the Sunday schools. These gifts were suitably acknowledged, by Mr. Wil- kinson, and a vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the proceedings to a close. PRESENTATION TO MRS. WILKINSON. On Sunday afternoon, on behalf of the teachers and scholars of the Girls' Sunday School, Kendrick-t., Mrs. Wilkinson was presented with a handsome Bible, prior to her departure this week for Thnperley. The Bible,which bore a suitable inscription, was presented on behalf of the subscribers by Mr. Joseph Lawless, the superinten- dent of the girls' school, who referred to Mrs. Wilkin- son's 18 years' services in the schools. It was true of Mrs. Wilkinson, as of her husband, that the best part of her life had been spent in the parish of St. Paul's. She had done a useful and noble work, and she had set a good example of regular attendance to teachers and scholars generally. They all sincerely wished her much happiness in her new sphere of labour. (Applause.) Mrs. Wilkinson suitably returned thanks, and the Vicar also acknowledged the compliment which had been paid to his wife.

Another letter has beeu r;:eived from MacDonald,now lying under sentence of death for the murder of Miss Holt in Longworth Clough. It is addressed to his aunt at Bolton, and is couched in most penitent terms. He hopes his aunt will not forget him in her prayers, and expresses himself quite resigned to his fate. He refers to his impending execution, and deplores he should have brought such disgrace upon his relatives.

div.head: MASONIC GATHERING.
div.p: MASONIC GATHERING.

INSTALLATION OF THE DUKE OF CLARENCE. An important Masonic gathering took place at the Town Hall, Reading, on Monday, when the Prince of Wales, as Grand Master, installed his son, the Duke of Clarence, as Provincial Grand Master for Berkshire, in succession to the late Sir Danial Gooch. Their Royal Highnesses journeyed by special train to Reading, and were received at the station by the Mayor and Corpora- tion, to whom they were introduced by Mr. Murdoch, M.P. for the borough. The Provincial Grand Lodge was opened at noon by the Prince of Wales, who performed the ceremony of installation. At the subsequent luncheon the Duke of Clarence presided. The Duke of Connaught proposed the health of the Prince of Wales. Lord Carrington, in responding for the visitors,conveyed greetings from 14,000 Freemasons in New South Wales. The town was decorated.

div.head: SITTING BULL RILLED. FIGHT WITH THE INDIANS.
div.p: SITTING BULL RILLED. FIGHT WITH THE INDIANS.
CAPTURE OF THE CAMP.

WASHINGTON, TtIESDAY.—An official despatch has been received here confirming the news of the death of Sitting Bull. The conflict occurred at ddybreak yesterday. Four of the police were killed and three others wounded, while the Indians lost eight men, including Sitting Bull. and his son Crowfoot. The troops are now in possession of Sitting Bull's camp, where the Indian women, chil- dren and property still remain. Sitting Bull's followers have, however, fled. . .

President Harrison, commenting on the above intellig- ence, paid that be had regarded Sitting Bull as the great disturbing element of the tribe. Now that this chief was dead, the President hoped that a settlement of the difficulties would be arrived at without further blood- shed.

NEW 'nits, TOESDAY.—Later intelligence from official sources, give further interesting particulars in respect to the Indian fighting. It seems that the Indians friendly to the authorities, who are acting as native police, pro- ceeded to Sitting Bull's camp, and arrested him on the ground that he was contemplating a breach of the peace. His followers, who were not numerous, attempted a res- cue, and the fighting mostly hand to hand, • was of a sharp and sanguinary character. Sitting Bull, the craftiest of all Indian leaders, was struck down early in the fray, and his son, who fought by his father's side, shared a similar fate. Two leading Sionxchiefs also fell, as well as six braves who formed a bodyguard round the old chief. Nevertheless, the Indians seem to have been prevailing against the Indian police, seven of whom had been shot or stabbed to death, when a body of a white troops arrived on the scene with a couple of Gatlings, which were speedily brought into play. The result was instantaneous, the hostile Indians scattering immedi- ately. The whites then advanced and captured the Indian village, securing at the same time Sitting Bull's body. _ _ _

/4W YORK, WEDNRSIDAY.—Fifteen dead bodies, the victims in Monday's fighting were brought to the Pine Ridge agency yesterday. Some time before he died, Sitting Bull said to General Miles, " God Almighty made me, God Almighty did not make me an agency [lndian. I'll fight and die fighting before any white man can make me an agency Indian." The Pine Ridge Indians will not talk of the death of Sitting Bull. They do not appear to be excited, but they are closely watched, and no unauthorised person is allowed to converse with them on the subject. A council of the chiefs of the friendly Indians is being held to consider the best action to take in regard to the Badland Indians. The only leader of Sitting Bull's band left is One Bull, and it is believed he will revenge his chief's death. In the fight on Monday, the Government lost some valuable men. The fight was short, and determined, and the Indians faced death firmly, believing that when the summer comes they will be restored to life under the new Messiah, and enjoy the luxuries of ancient times, when game abounded and white men were unknown. ANOTHER BATTLE.

HEAVY LOSS OF' UNITED STATES CAVALRY. DIiNVBR, Wammsnay.—The following telegram has been received from Rapid City, Dakota :—A rancher who Las arrived here reports that a body of cavalry has been attacked by Indians, and two officers and fifty mzn killed. The Indians were repulsed with heavy loss, but the exact number of casualties on their side has not yet been ascertained. Uncertainty also prevails as to the particular force which was attacked, but it is thought probable that it may be that under the command of Major Tupper, of the 6th Regiment. It consisted of three troops, numbering 140 men. A force of cavalry from Rapid City will march to-day to the assistance of the troops that have been in action.

div.head: TECHNICAL EDUCATION. PROPOSED SCHEME FOR WARRINGTON
div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION. PROPOSED SCHEME FOR WARRINGTON

The Library and Museum Committee have had the question of technical education for Warrington under considkration, and the following report on the subject was adopted by the Committee with a view to he being approved by the Town Council at the next monthly meeting:— REPORT ON SETB-COMMITTEE ON 'TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION. Your Sub-Committee having carefully considered the subject referred to, begs to report that in its opinion it is most desirable to provide systematic technical instruc- tion in Warrington. A draft scheme has accordingly been prepared, which the Sub-Committee considers will meet all the requirements of the town in this direction, so far as the existing law enables the Town Council to deal with them. A copy of it is appended to this report. It is based upon the assumption that a sum of (say) £7OO a year will be contributed by the county of Lancaster. The County Councils have at their dis- Plsal (under the provisions of the Local Taxation Act, 1890) a large sum of money derived from Imperial taxa- tion, which they may if they choose apply to the provi- sion of technical instruction, and it may be assumed as certain that if the fund is so used the grant will be con- tinued by Parliament from year to year. It is very pro- bable, though not yet decided, that the Lancashire County Council will so apply the proportion allotted to this county, but the Sub-Committee believes that it is of the utmost importance that steps should be taken at once to enable the town to share in the distribution of this year's grant. It is therefore recommended that the Town Council be moved to authorise this Committee to proceed with the necessary arrangements. The Sub- Committee anticipates that it will not be found neces- sary to incur any expenditure for new buildings at first, but that the accommodation already existing in the town will suffice for a considerable development of the move- ment. Some initial expenditure for special furniture may perhaps be required, but, with that exception, and un til the institution is fairly established, it will be possible to carry on a very extensive work without any assis- tance from the Borough Fund.—Signed, on behalf of the Sub-Committee, F. MONKS, Chairman. Warrington, 10th December, 1890. SCHEME FOR A TECHNICAL SCHOOL
The following draft scheme for the establishment of a Technical School accompanies the report. It is merely a draft, and is subject of course to such modifications as circumstances may suggest:—

The Museum and Library Commitiee tOTake over the School of Art, and become responsible for science and art Waching in the borough, in -connection with the Free Fpblic Library and Museum. To establish a complete technical School for day and evening students, to be opeued to all classes of both sexes, above (say) 13 years, who shall have passed through the 6th standard in any elementary school, or shall pass the entrance examination required. The fees for day scholars not to exceed (say) a 2s. per annum for those who Mt for the science and art examinations, and £5 ss. for those who do not sub- mit to the examination. To establish scholarships of (say) £lO a year, with a free education for two years open to both sexes.

IT was LEIGH HUNT who said that, "A Merry " kindness is the best of all Christmas." truths." It is an aphorism which ' has its origin in the preaching of the doctrine of peace on earth and good-will to men. We hear not a little of that doctrine during Christmas-tide and it is a pity that we do not hear more of it at other tides. We must, however, be thankful for the good the gods provide, and make the most there- fore of Christmas. Whatever it may be to those well on in life who have,on the way, dropped many illusions, it is undoubtedly a season of real rejoic- ing to children; for their imaginations are fresh and their fancies are free. "Merry goes the world when the heart is young," and it never goes mer- rier than at Christmas time. A few shillings—or few pence even--judiciously spent,may be the means of brightening the lives of the young for many a day. Thanks to the progress of art as revealed in a hundred ways, nice things need not now be confined to the homes of the rich. Toys, books, and cards are "beautiful exceedingly," and they are now produced at prices which are practically within the reach of every working-man. It is true that there is luxury in art, and that art was never - more luxurious than it is to-clay. But it is a great mistake to suppose that increase in the price of a thing necessarily means an in- crease in the enjoyment to be derived from it. Granted that there is a certainty that the wolf will be kept from the door, it is a matter of course to say that the poor will have a jollier time than the rich during What is known as the festive season. They are more truly social; their interest in each other is more genuine; they are not afraid to laugh outright at any little thing that pleases them; and, as the song has it, "laughing is con- tagious, and sometimes advantageous." There are, to be sure, people amongst all classes who take life seriously, and look upon every Christmas as a stage nearer the charnel house. Life to them is a vale of tears, and they would have everybody oc- cupied in wiping their eyes. But the true philo- sopher is illustrated by the story of the laughter- loving priest, before whom a bonfire was lighted, while a solemn brother exclaimed, "Thus pass the pomps and vanities of this wicked world." "But whilst they pass," said the merry soul, suiting the action to the word, "let us warm our hands." Yes, let us warm our hands, and let others have a chance of sharing the warmth. One of the worst tendencies of this wealth- : creating age is that of the separation of classes. For hundreds of years, and until, in fact, the last : half century, it was the custom of employers to ; dwell amongst their workpoople. They were thus necessarily in touch with them—in the home as in the mill; there was a strong bond of sympathy which resulted in what Shelley calls— " The little nameless unremembered acts Of kindness and of love." To-day a wholly different order of things prevails. • The growth of population has caused the workers

to herd more closely and unhealthily together: and the growth of wealth has enabled the em— ployer to seex health far from city smoke and far from the madding crowd. This is good for him and for his family, but It is not good for the com- munity as a whole. It has brought about the separa- tion of classes; and relaxed the friendly bond between master and man. The remedy for this is as yet afar off; but meantime we may preserve ' and cultivate the amenities of. Christmas-tide as a means, for a time at any rate, of drawing men closer together with a feeling that, whatever may be the difference of social station) we
I,

are all of one flesh and blood, it, as there is good authority for saying, it is more blessed to give than to receive, the well-to-do have a special opportunity of showering blessings upon them- selves at this season of the year. There is, of course, such a thing as pauperising, but there are numerous methods of giving a lift on the way without the effect being other than wholly good. Food and warmth are necessaries of life when the weather is severe ; and where there is a lack of either the word enjoyment is a mockery. Gifts in kind are, therefore, after all the kindest gifts; but, and let us say it in all earnestness, it is not a help— it is a hindrance to give intoxicating liquor. It is a custom" more honoured in the breach than in tte observance ;" and it is a custom we are glad to know which finds less favour year by year. The prospects this year of "A merry Christmas" are, on the whole, favourable ; trade is good, and promises to con- tinue good; and that means that there is work to be had, with a tendency for wages to rise. It is true the weather is severe ;it is what is called "an old fashioned winter," which means an old fashioned way of laying up the old and tho feeble. But the cold may be fought and beaten with extra cloaks, coats, blankets and coals, and is in the hope that none of our readers will be lacking in these things needful that we cordially wish them the most hearty enjoyment of the Yuletide.

'Tue struggle Au. eyes are turned on the struggle in for supremacy which is going on Ireland. amongst Home Rulers in Ireland. Exceptional interest is being taken in the Kilkenny contest which will be decided on Monday next. Mr. PARNELL got the start as the man in posses- sion of the machinery of the Land League ; and he made "a brave show " last week in Dublin and Cork. But the signs are increasing that the majority in the country is against him—just as it is in the Parliamentary party. Mr. DAVITT is on his track, and it is now war to the knife between the two. Both have already personally suffered as a result of the affrays which have taken place be- tween the Parnellites and the Nationalists ; Mr. DAVITT has felt the weight of blackthorns on his head and shoulders, arid Mr. PARNELL has been hit on the face with a bag of limo which temporarily blinded him. It is much to be regretted that there ishould be anything in the nature of violence ; but Irishmen are Irishmen and there aro times when they wil/ argue with sticks. The late chief of the Nationalists is either losing his head in the fierce conflict, or ho has made up his mind to rowdy it out with the worst of them. It j„s part of his present stock-in-trade to speak of Ms opponents as "gutter-sparrows,"" miserable scum," 4‘ fools," and " lunatics." We are inclined to think that he is getting "groggy "—to borrow a sporting ,brase—and that his language beopi.cs, pimplier ts his hold bee6ille§ Weaker. Yie has left the lofty pedestal of the hero who was to have Ireland at his feet and dictate terms. There was something

almost sublime in the imperious way in which he sought to ignore the Divorce Decree as the origin of the present troubles. This was all very well so long as he was at meetings within four walls, and surrounded by ardent supporters. But oh! the difference when he has to address friend and foe in the village market-place! What Mr. T. HEALY called "the stench of the Divorce court" is brought under his nose ; and it is to be hoped it will be kept there until he retires from the field as sick of it as all decent, honest people are sick of him and his moral and political delinquencies. The outrageous way in which Mr. PARNELL seized upon "United Ireland" in the absence of Mr. W. O'BRIEN, the editor, has turned many Irishmen against him, and greatly embittered the conflict. But already the arch-mischief-maker has been met by a " Sup- pressed United Ireland" which is being sent broadcast through the country. It contains an important letter from Archbishop WALsn, who puts the case against Mr. PARNELL in a nutshell when he says he has broken his pledge, which was "to sit, act and vote with the Irish Parliamen- tary party." He adds :—" If any member of the party no longer feels himself conscientiously free to sit, to act, to vote with the party, he can go back to his constituents, and if a new party is to be formed upon the basis of allegiance to an in- dividual leader, he can become a member of it." Thisis a just and fair way of stating the issue; and it disposes at a stroke of the nonsensical sup- position that the pledge taken was a pledge to Mr. Parnell. It sets the cause above the man; and lowers the late leader of the Nationalists to the level of other unworthy sons of Ireland who have in the past broken their pledges and dishonoured themselves and their country.

The Repulse IT cannot be a matter of surprise at to anybody that, in the present Bassetlaw. state of affars in Ireland, the Liberals have failed to win a seat in one of the Tory strongholds of Nottinghamshire; but it is disappointing to find that the Conservative candi- date has won with an increased majority of over 400. It is a repulse in the great struggle, but it is not a defeat. Those who are on the spot, and ought therefore to be in a position to form an opinion, attribute a large proportion of the decrease in the poll to the severity of the weather, which especially operated against the Liberals, who were ill sup- plied with private conveyances as compared with the Conservatives. The figures have, at any rate, no tale to tell of Conservative growth. There has been no contest in the Basset- law Division since 1865, and meantime the Tories have had added unto them the peculiar people known as Dissentient Liberals. Yet what is the result? The Tory candidate for 1890 polls only 14 votes more than :the Tory can- didate for 1885, and this, too, in face of the divi- sion amongst Irish Home Rulers! What has hap- pened is what, to a certain extent, was expected— there has beena falling off in the Liberal poll, the Liberal candidate obtaining 419 votes less than the Liberal who contested the seat in 1885. The decline is the result oi Liberal abstentions, not of a transference of votes from one ,party to the other. Bad weather and lack of conveyances may account for something; but it is highly pro- bable that a considerable proportion of the electors who have failed to poll would have risked the inclem- ency ef the weather—footing it all the way—if their enthusiasm had not been damped by the state of affairs in Ireland. What has happened at Basset- law is of a piece with ivliat took place at Warring- ton and in Manchester in the IVlunicipal elections which have occurred &ince Mr. PARNELL was dis- covered to be no longer worthy to bo the leader of the Irish or any other psople. The situation is discouraging; but it is not ono to occasion despair. A storm may arise when a vessel is within sight of the port, and it is as much the duty of the cap- tain and crew to battle with it as if it had come upon them at the beginning of the voyage. Home Rule is the port to which the good ship of Liberal- ism is musing, and there is no call to turn asido because of an unexpected gale. It will blow over as other storms have done; the vessel will right it-
sell; and enter the harbour—somewhat delayed— but with colours flying and amid welcoming cheers.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
There once was a man called Parnell, Who got on uncommonly well, Until, more's the pity, He went courting Kitty— Kind Kitty O'Shea—and he fell To the depths of the nethermost hell.

Some of the big drapery firms in London, are agreeing to give their assistants a four-days holi- day at Christmas ; they are to be released from duty from Wednesday night until Monday morn- ing. This is "something like ;" it will enable the young people to travel hundreds of miles, and have a good time with the old folks at home.

It appears that the brief but lively sketch of Mr. Monks, which appeared in the American papers, whilst our townsman was on a visit to that country, was from the pen of Mr. James Bate,forrnerly assistant in the Warrington Library, and now on the staff of "Chicago Herald." Mr. Bate is making headway on the press; and, seeing that he described Mr. Monks as a millignaire, there is no denying his use of the faculty of imagination.

"Where are we working now? " The first London line worked by electricity commenced operations, without fuss or formality, on Thursday morning. It is an underground line ; there is only one class, and one fare, and tickets are there- fore dispensed with. It is likely to prove a great success, and gives a promise of the time when, as Byron has it, " steam "—or, as he would now say, electric "engines shall conduct us to the moon."

On the first of January a new publication entitled " Our Magazine "is to be issued. It will deal with subjects for thought and discussion in social and political clubs, reading and lecture rooms, debating societies, Co-operative meeting rooms, 4c,; and, as the price is twopence only, it ought to adult/land a large sale. It is to be published by Messrs. Simpkin, Marshall and Co., and, judging from the advance copy which has reached us, it will be in every way worthy of support.

Speaking at a banquet in London, on Tuesday night, Sir Henry James went beyond the mark in saying as to Mr. Parnell that "all that was now known was equally well known in 1886." Surely there had been no divorce decree then ? And as to other matters, why does Sir Henry fix on the year 1886? Is it because it would be inconvenient to say 1885, seeing that was the year when the Tories were in alliance with tho Irish Nationalists ?

Mr. J. K. Stephen, son of Mr. Justice Stephen, was to have been the Tory candidate for North Kilkenny, but drew back at the last moment. He is more candid than many of his party, for on being questioned to as whether he favoured Mr. Parnell, _ _

lie said :—" Yes, I support him as the best way to iiamage Home Rule.' This side-light ought to be a revelation to Irish Home Rulers, and Cause them tq drop Mr, F'arnell like the provovbial hot potatoes

'Pamell's abuse of Sir John ifennessy as the Nationalist candidate for Kilkenny, shows, per- haps better than anything else, how unscrupulous he has become in the desperate straits in which he finds himself. Until Mr. Parnell was deposed, Sir John was before the country as Mr. Parnell's nominee; and it is only since be has thrown in his lot with the Irish Parliamentary Party that Mr. Parnell has discovered Sir Johns unfitness. But it won't do; criticism of this kind is so thin that everybody can see through it.

It is to be feared that the Deposed Chief will hurt his friends as well as his foes—he strikes so blindly. introducing Mr. Harrison to a meeting the other day, he said :—" Mr. Harrison is the only man who has fought the police singin-handed at Tipperary, and choked three of them." This was intended to go down with "the boys," and it did go down; but it is a poor way of serving the young M.P., seeing that the issue is still to be tried, and that, EQ far from assaulting the police, Mr. Harrison has already swom that it was the police who assaulted him.

The Recorder of Liverpool has taken a course of his own in inflicting short sentences ; and it would appear that certain justices are disposed to restore the balance by going to the other extreme. Mr. Justice Williams astonished a Chester jury last week, by sentencing a woman to five years servitude for perjury! There is a movement for getting the sentence reduced, and, although perjury is too lightly treated, as a rule, in courts of justice it is to be hoped that the punishment in this case will be mitigated. Five months would have been better than five years.

A builder at Garston has been fined 40s. and costs for using inferior material while putting up dwelling houses. It is a relief to know that what is sometimes described as " jerry building can be put a stop to by enforcing bye-laws. Are there any bye-laws in Warrington? And do they war- rant the erection of closets to front a public thoroughfare, and in a line with the houses in the street? These are questions which should be put tit the next Council meeting. "Someone has blundered," at Heath-side, and the blunder should be brought home, and rectified.

On Tuesday "The World" announced that the Queenhad "reconsidered her former answer," and had definitely promised to inaugurate the Man- chester Ship Canal "during the autumn." The works of the canal are, it is stated on the same authority, advancing far more rapidly than was anticipated; and the "Mayor, Mr. J. Mark, is already considering with his colleagues the various details of the Royal visit." This is altogether a very pretty story; but there is reason to believe that it is a "story "; the Mayor of Manchester is not considering what to do, for he knows nothing about the matter.

Mr. Herbert Ward, who was an officer of Mr. Stanley's Rear Guard, lectured on Central Africa, at Earlestown, on Monday evening; but he care- fully abstained from expressing- any opinion on the atrocities of the late Major Barttelot. He shows himself circumspect in not making this hideous topic a portion of his lecture; but it occupied the minds of those who listened to him—particularly when he spoke of civilization being the means of abolishing the barbarities at present practiced. If the natives who suffered at the hands of the whites could have been present they would prob- ably have asked for less civilisation and more , humanity.

General Booth visited St. Helens, on Wednes- day. He addressed a conference in the afternoon, and a public meeting in the evening, and made a favourable impression. There is no gainsaying the fundamental principle of his scheme, namely, that "there ought to be work of a remunerative char- acter for every man and woman in the country who is willing to work." If provision is made for this, and if nothing more be accomplised, it will be a good thing done which will bo well Worth the money which is proposed to be spent. There willbe failures in some respects in workine• out the details; but, when men are capable and actuated by worthy motives, failures are the stepping stones to sue- ZEISS.

It is as well to see ourselves at times as others see us. A Turkish paper has been contrasting Christianity and Mohammedanism; and this ishow tilt writer hits out :—" What is this progress of civilisation ' that. the Europeans speak of ? It means that success justifies everything. To lie, to cheat, or to ffog and hang starving Mussulmans like Stanley's rear-guard for stealing a mouthful of meat is justified by it. The motto 'Clear out for I want to come there' is justified by it, and is illustrated by the destruction of native races wher- ever Europeans set foot." There is a good dcial of truth in this; but couldn't as black a ease be made out against the slave-stealing Niusselmans What it all -comes to is this, that, creed or no creed, human nature is pretty much the same all;the world over.

Wright, eldest son of Mr. Thomas Wright, of Halton, has passed the second examination in the medical and surgical degrees for the B.A. degree. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN. On Sunday evening the Rev. J. Simpson preached a sermon on General Booth's "Darkest England," and at the close a collection was made in aid of the General's Scheme. Nearly £5 was realised. HONOUR FOR A WIDNES ENGINEER. At a recent meeting of the Institute of Civil Engineers, Mr. Thomas Allen Bullough, of the Widnes Alkali works, who resides at Peelhouse-lane, Farnworth, was elected an associate member (A.M.1.C.E.) with full corporate privileges.

Mr. Gornall is the son of Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer of Health for Warrington. ACME DOOR CHECKS AND SPRINGS.—G arlaud, Ironmonger, Earlestown and Warrington.—Adrt. ILLNESS OF LORD CREWE.

Lord Crewe, who is staying at Crewe Hall, his Cheshire seat, has been exceedingly ill during the past week, and his condition has caused considerable anxiety. The death of Lord Tollemache came as a great shock to Lord Crewe, the two Cheshire noble- men being great friends. On inquiring at Crewe Hall, on Tuesday, a correspondent was informed that Lord Crewe was somewhat better. THE COLLIERS' STRIKE AT ECCLESTON.

The dispute between the colliers and their em- ployers at the Eccleston Hall collieries, which has been .previously referred to, remains unsettled. Two or three weeks ago the men struck work in consequence of the alteration in the system of pay. On Saturday,3lr. Glover, miners' agent, waited upon the proprietors and on behalf of the men offered to accept 4s. 3d., but the masters refused to offer more than 3s. 6d., consequently the strike continues PLEURO-PNEUMONIA IN LA.NCASIIIRE.

Monday night's "London Gazette "states that an area at Bold, near St. Helens, Lancashire, is infected with pleuro-pneumonia. A further order notifies that "a scheduled district comprising so much of the County of Lancaster as lies to the south and south-east of the River Ribble, and also comprising the boroughs of Accrington, Ashton-under-Lyne, Bacup, Blackburn. Bolton, Bootle-cum-Linacre, Burnley, Bury, Chorley, Clitheroe, Darwen, Hey- wood, Liverpool, Manchester, Middleton, Mossley, Nelson, Oldham, Itochdale, St. Helens, Salford, Southport, Watrington and Wigan " is &so infected.

div.p: CHURCH PARADE AT RUNCORN.

The Runcorn companies of the Earl of Cliesters' Rifles held their annual church parade on Sunday. The corps mustered at the Drill Hall and walked to the Parish ' Church accompanied by the band. The Rev. Canon Wood. vicar, preached an appropriate sermon. PRESENTATION TO MR. E. W. Ilimonnays, ov RUNCORN. At the annual social meetiry, of the Moss Side (Man-: cheater) Musical and Literar;Society, held on Wednes- day evening, a presentation was made t ) Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys and Mrs. Humphreys, of Runcorn, in com- memoration of their marriage, and in recognition of Mr. liumphrefs services to the Society. Mr. Humphrey:4 was formerly a vice president of the Society. The pre- sent took the farm of a chaste biscuit cannister, made of cathedral glass, %Kith gold and silver mounting. IF DESERTION AT WIDNES. '

Michael Devereausi, 18, Waring-street, was summoned before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, for desert- ing his wife Margarek. Mrs. Devereaux said she had been married to the tlefenclant for 27 years, and had had ,13 children, five of whom she had to support. Defend- ant went away nine weeks ago, and since then she had not received any money from him.—The Bench ordered defendant to pay 10s. a week towards the support of his family, but lie left the court asserting that he would go to gaol first. ROT WATER. HP:ATM.—Garland sends estimates free. Warrington.—Advt.

SCHOLARSHIP AT FAIINWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL. The Governors of Farnworth Grammar School offer annually for competition amongst boys from elementary schools in the ancient Chapelry of Farnworth, two free scholarships tenable for three years at Faxnworth Grammar School. There were 16 competitors at the examination held recently,and the scholarships, it is now announced, have been won by John P. Hughes, of 30, Ross-st., and Thos. A. Bottomlev, of 63, Halton View, pupils at Sinn's Cross and Warrington-road Board Schools respectively.

GREENWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOODS, RUNCORN. The scholars attending the above schools were, yester- day week, treated to another of the series of magic lan- tern entertainments, which are b-:ing given by the teachers, during the winter months. Stanley's travels through "Darkest Africa" formed the subject of the S ancl entertainment, and afterwards a large number of comic Elides were shown to the great amusement of the young- stem ong hymns were sung at intervals during the evening, Tile lautern was skilfully mani- pulated by Mr. W. CHRISTMAS ARRANGEMENTS AT RUNCORN Posr OFFICE. The large increase of postal business incidental to the Christmastide, renders necessary special arrangements so that the local staff can cope with the immense num- ber of missives despatched and received, Theref.,.;te on Christmas eve the letter box at the head office will close a quarter of an hour earlier than Usual, viz., 8.30 p.m., but by attaching an extra halfpenny stamp to inland letters, and ld, to foreign letters, they may be posted up to 8.45. There Is no late fee for local letters for Runcorn, Weston Point and Halton posted up to 9 p.m, The business on Christmas day will be carried son the same as Sunday. NOT NROLECT DRINKING FOR WORK. At Runcorn Police Court. on Wednesday, befne Mr. John Brundrit and Dr. Steele, John Andrews, a labourer, was brought up on a warrant charged with neglecting his wife and four children. He pleaded guilty, and M.r. Ward, the relieving officer, stated the mans 'family were inmates of the Workhouse. They had previcilisty been relieved from time to time. The prisoner was able to earn 245. a week, but he" would not neglect drink- ing for work."—The prisoner said he was willing to pay towards the maintenance of his family in the work- h )use, but Mr. Ward replied that the Workhouse was not a lodging honse.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to 14 days' hard labour. &MACE( .0E WIDNES BYELAWS. At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Thomas Cook, Alforde-st., was summoned by the Widnes Local Board, for contravening section 11 of the byelaws. Mr. J. T. Allen (clerk) prosecuted,and said the defendant was summoned for keeping a pig in his back yard,which was within fifty yards from his dwelling house. The byelaws referred to, he said, had been advertised throughout the township in December, 1888,calling attention to the fact that if it was contravened the offender was liable to a penalty of £5 and costs, and 403. and costs for every day a. person continued to offend after the notice had been served by the inspector. John Dickson, nuisance in- spector, proved to finding the pig in the back yard, which was within the prescribed distance. He had warned the defendant before. The defendant's wife said the pig in question had got the cramp, and had been removed from the cote to allow of it being treated with paraffin oil. The leach dismissed the case on Mrs- Cook promising not to repeat the offence. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest, notioe.l.,-7.. a W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et.. Warrington. —.Advt.

1317RGLARY BY A DRDNEEN MAN, AT WIDNES. Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. W. Deacon, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Michael Glynn, a la- I bourer at West Bank Dock, was charged with breaking and entering the office of Mr. G. E. Sayce, stevedore at West Bank Dock, and stealing therefrom a tin box I containing several books and money amounting to £5 I les. The office was securely locked up on Thursday I afternoon, and on Friday morning, Mr. J. 11. Sayce, brother to the prosecutor, discovered that the officedoor had been broken open. The tin boz, which contained books, a bag of silver, and a bag of copper, had been I previously found under the railway arch, by .a plate- layer named George Wood, of Ditton. The bag of cwer had been taken, but the bag of silver, worth £5 14s.,was untouched. 'On Friday afternoon the prisoner met P.C. Robinson, in Waterloo-road, and made a ,confessisn to him. He said on Thursday night he got drunk at the Arch Hotel, and having spent all his money, he went to Mr. Sayce's office and broke open the door with a rail- way chair. Ho carried the tin bast under the arches, where he forced the lock and took a bag containing some coppers, leaving the box lying there. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. He was allowed bail, himself in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each.

TREAT TO TRH WORKHOUSE CHH.DREN AT DUTTON. Through the kindness of Mrs. Soulby (principal of Greve House School, Runcorn), the children of the Dutton Workhouse were provided with a tea and Christmas tree on Wednesday. The tree. which had been presented by Mr. Hervey Talbot, of Aston Hall, was decorated during the afternoon by Mrs. and Miss Soulby, Miss Pierpoint, and a number of the older pupils, the branches being , laden with pretty presents for the children. At four o'clock the children sat down to a stfostantial tea consist- ing of ham sandwiches, bun loaf, &c. They went waited upon by the young ladies of Grove House, and after re- galing themselves to their hearts' content with the many good things provided, they repaired to their respective wards until six o'clock when all the inmates and children were grouped together round the Christmas tree, which stood in the entrance hall. When lighted up, the tree presented a very handsome appearance. The presents were afterwards distributed by Mrs. ,Soulby. Through the generosity of the same lady all the women of the " house " received tea and sugar, and the men tobacco. A quantity of sweets and oranges was also brought for the Children. Later in the evening an entertainment of a varied and amusing nature was tendered by the Rev . Jos. Holden's Temperance Minstrel Tronpe" of the Parish Church, Runcorn, under the leadership of Mr. Clare. The chair was taken by Mr. I. Talbot, who wasaccompanied by Mrs. Talbot. A large number of invitations had been sent out by the master of the" house," Mr. :T. Cunnah to numerous friends and neighbours, who with very few exceptions, availed themselves of the privilege. At ten o'clock the entertainment was brought to a close. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Semlby and to Mr. Holden for their kindness, after which the inmates retired.

Severe weather is reported from all parts of the coun- try, causing much suffering. A shocking murder was discoveled on Monday morn- ing. at Barrandarritlgr, about five miles from Wicklow, the victim being a widow named Lyons who kept a small shop. The murderer is believed to be a tramp.

div.head: SINGULAR ACCIDENT TO A GAS STOKER,.
div.p: SINGULAR ACCIDENT TO A GAS STOKER,.

On Saturday nil-it,--slio.;tl3Tr-iitt.:r—t-w—el.;;Olciock, a singular and serious accident befel a man in charge of the Ashton Local Board Gas Works. It appears that Derbyshire, who was on the night turn, was engaged in his usual duties during the first part of the night ; when, owing to the frost, several of the lights about the works would not burn, and he was compelled to light two stand grate tires as he could / not see his way about. At the tittle named, one of I the syphons to the condensers blew out, owing to the pipe being frozen, and Derbyshire at once went to attend to it. Whilst thus engaged, the wind blew the gas escaping directly into the stand grate Itre, with the result that the gas exploded, and Derbyshire was very severely burnt about the face. There being no one about, the poor fellow had to struggle on in the keen frost until relieved by the next turn, during which time be suffered dread- fully. He is, however, improving, lthouo still suffering from the effects of the frost in the

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Hanicinson, W. Handley, H. J. Grice, T. Riley, and Dr. MacLennan with J. D. Jones (librarian).

div.head: TRE COMMITTEE AND THE COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: TRE COMMITTEE AND THE COMMISSIONERS.

A letter was read from Mr. Marshall, secretary to the Commissioners, informing the Committee that their recommendation to free the library premises from the charge of rent was rejected by the Commissioners.—The Chairman: Nobody supported it, did they? Mr. (irice : No.—The Chairman: Mr. Humphreys, who was the ori- ginator, was unable to be present, and he had sent a communication stating that he wa a unable to be present that day also, so that it was hardly worth while going into the matter further.—Mr. Handley said he noticed from the newspapers that it was attempted to be proved that the Committee were not able to spend all the money voted, because they had a balance at the end of the year until it was pointed out by the auditor that this was not legal, and it was insinuated that in consequence, the Committee determined to spend all their money, and purchased things that the town did not really need.—Mr. Hankinson remarked that that only referred to one particular occa- sion.—The Librarian said there was no member knew more about the matter than Mr. Handley, because it was he that he (Mr. Jones) fetched when the auditor threatened to sequester the balance. He was simply at his wits ends, and Mr. Handley showed the auditor how the things really stood. After the meeting of the Com- missioners he consulted the annual reports for the past &gilt years. When the library was established, he found that the number of books issued was 155,437. There was a decrease reported last year, but unfortunately, in the printed report, the decrease was shown 173 instead of 173. This was really a cause for congratulation, because those people who, the previous year, read novels, took out the heavier books the succeeding year in conse- quence of the University Extension Lectures. The rea- son why the Committee had such large balances, before the auditor threatened to hand over the balance to the General Fund, was because the Commissioners never handed over the balance of the rate less the rent, until Lady Hay, and the auditor suggested that in future the Library Committee should ask for a portion of the rate periodically after estimating the amount required. Dur- ing the eight years, he found the amount spent on new books was £sot 19s. 2d .; book binding £163 Bs. 9d.; news- papers and magazines. £144 10s. 2d.; fittings, £l4l Os. 11d.; rent, heating, lighting,and cleaning, £196 16s. The Chairman said it seemed to hum an entirely false deduc- tion from the facts, that because there were not so many books taken out in one yeara.s another, that therefore no new books were needed. It was when books got old and stale that people did not take them out.—The Librarian said he forgot to 'mention that the year before last the increase in the issue was abnormal—something likethree or four thousand more than the previous year. So that it was not bad to have only a decrease of 173.—Mr. Han- ley said probably one outcome of the discussion would be an application for the price of land adjoining that build- ing. He felt certain that they would soon have a build- ing that would answer for Library purposes and is school of ecience and Art, and he believed tile inhabitants of Runcorn would be glad to aid this advance in the right ' direction.
THE LIBRARY. It was stated that the suo-Committee appointed to arrange for the more frequent opening of the Library had not yet prepared the report.

_ _ STATISTICS. The monthly report showed that during November the Librarrwas open on 13 occasions, and a total of 1,978 hooks was issued, a decrcase of 195. They were classi- fied as fonows : theology. 43, philosophy., 10. Science, 92, history &c., 194, poetry, 14, fiction, 1443, miscellaneous, 182. In the reference department there had been 12 books consnited. a, decrease of 64 compared vrah the corresponding month last year. "DARKEST EY:OLAND " _ _

On the proposition of Mr. Elandley, seconded hr Mr. Grine. it was resolved to purchase two copies of General Booth's work, "Darkest England and the way out, the hooks to be laid on the reading room table and tact removed.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.

BY "AN OCCASIONAL COIMESPONDRNV2 The action of Widnes Local Board at theit lee meeting, in requesting Mr. Eustace Carey to with. draw his letter of resignation will meet with gene- ral approval. As a member of that body he hat given 16 years of his life to the service of the rate- payers, and no inconsiderable part of the town's work bears the impress of his character and ability. Dr. O'Keeffe and Mr. Carey have occasionally had sharp passages on matters of policy, but the former clearly saw that Mr. Carey's retirement would be a distinct loss to the ratepayers, and he took the initiative in an endeavour to obtain the withdrawal of the resignation. It is to be hoped that Mr. Carey will accede to the unanimous wish of the Board. It is a matter of regret that Mr. ll.Linaker, the able and respected Clerk of Runcorn Union,is confines' to his residence through ill-health, and finds himself compelled to relinquish a portion of his duties. He desires to be relieved of the work of the Rural Sanitary Authority, and, the law providing that the assistant clerk shall act in his absence, Mr. Livaker wishes that course to be taken. As Mr. Aaron and other members pointed out, the Authority are at present involved in business of the utmost impor- tance with the Ship Canal Compsny, and they feel that Mr. Linaker's advice by reason of his long and varied experience, and his ability, will be necessary to a successful termination of the impending nego- tiations. Under these circumstances Mr. Linaker will, no doubt, sink his personal feelings and con- venience, and though the way be hard, continue in the path of duty, along which he has travelled SO faithfully and well for so many lung years. The scheme for providing Runcorn with a Tech- nical Institute, which was propounded at a special meeting of the Commissioners this week, will be read with the utmost interest by the ratepayers. Such an institute would be of the utmost benefit to the rising generation, and, as Mr. Pritchard ex- plained, the terms of the Technical Institution Act are so wide, that all the advantages of a good 1 secondary school can be secured under its provi- sions, a matter for sincere congiatulations. It would appear that the extent and scope of the scheme will be affected in some degree by the amount of grant obtained from the special fund controlled by the County Council, and we hope that body will deal with the application made to them in a generous spirit. Fortunately, Mr. Speakman is a member of the County Technical Education Committee, and he will be in a position to personally advocate the claims of his native town. That success may attend the applications and any efforts Mr. Speakman may make will be the wish of all interested in education.
The Widnes Local Board have now made an application to the proper quarter for a Charter of Incorporation, and the " Chemical Metropolis " is one step nearer attaining the dignity of a borough.

div.head: – – – WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: - - - WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB.

The first lecture of the season was held in the large room of the Widnea Liberal Club on Thursday night, when Mr. T. Snape, C.C.. dealt with the sub- ject of " Our National Debt." Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, J.P., presided, and there was a large and apprecia- tive aldience.

The Chairman in introducing Mr. Snape, said that it was exceedingly important that from time to time our attention should be very strongly drawn to matters con- nected with our system of taxation. They were all as frail mortals apt to forget figures, and the great thing they must try and do was to grasp the princi- ples which underlay the figures and the facts upon which the figures were based. It was most important that they should do this because a really good system of taxation lay at the root of all good government and it was generally admitted—by Liberals at all events—that our present system of taxation required a great deal of reform. It would be necessary some day in future to try and make a considerable improvement in the incidence of taxation and lift the burdens from the shoulders of the poorer portion of the population on to those wbo are better able to bear the burden. (Applause.)—He added that the outrageous manner in which the national debt was piled up was a standing disgrace to class legislation. (Applause.)—Mr. Snape, expressed his pleasure that they were assemblEd under the presidency of a towns- man so justly respected r:s Mr. H. Wade Deacon. (Ap- plause.) They were looking forward with the greatest possible confidence to the expectation of seeing him, as soon as an opportunity arrived, elected as their re- presentative in Parliament. (Applause.) Dealing with his subject, Mr. Snape said the national debt last year amounted to a little under 700 millions of money having been reduced during the past five or six years by over 40 millions through the operation of what are called terminable annuities. He showed how this tremendous debt had been accumulated though in the main throughiwarfare, only half a crown in the £of the whole national debts of Europe, having been caused by productive purposes; generally wars were pieces of folly and barren of beneficial results. The principle he should like to see acted upon was that those who made quarrels should be the only ones to fight and also the only ones to pay.—The usual vote of thanks was accorded.

div.p: HEALTH OF THE D2STRICT.

The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams) iePOAed an outbreak of diptheria at Frodsham, Halsbv, and pointed out a serious nuisance at Collier's Square, lielsby. Meask had broken out at Stockton Heath. and a large propor- tion of school children were affected. 40 or 50 cases at least had occurred.

_ THE POLLUTION OF EECKIWICK BROOK. Mr. Aaron asked if anything had yet been heard from the Local Government Board vrith regard to the pollution of lieekwiek Brook.—TheDepay Clerk said a letter was read a fortnight ago, in which the Board said they were not in a position to reply.—Mr. Aaron said if the Au; ho- rity neglected their business like the Local Government Board were neglecting this matter, they would be quickly censured. The stream was polluted with poison- ous refuse,.and it would be in that condition next sum- mer unless something was done, and cattle would be dy- ing as in the past.. He proposed that a sharp letter in- deed be sent to the head quartets..—Mr. Heywood se- conded.—The Deputy Clerk said the letters to the Local Government Board were always aodrassed to the Presi- dent.—The motion was carried unanimously.
RESIGNATION OF THE CLERK.

The Chairman said he had received a letter from Mr. Linaker, which the members, he was sure, would be grieved to hear. It read as follows: "Being unable, owing to the state of my health,: to give that personal attention to the duties of the clerk of the Authority which I think they require, I would thank you to bring this letter before the Authority at theineeting to-morrow, arid ask them to appoint the assistant clerk to the Guar- dians, the clerk to the Authority under section 190 of the Public Health Act, 1875. I shall at sil times be pleased to give every assistance I can with a view to the work being carried out satisfacterily. I am, dear sir, yours faithfully, 11. Linaker."—The Chairinan said the clause referred to stated that "if. the clerk was unable or

unwilling to take such additional duty (Rural Sani- tary Authority) the assistant clerk of the Union shall be appointed to discharge the same with such remunera- tion as aforesaid." Under the circumstances it was im- perative that they shonld appoint the assistant clerk ; but he thought the matter had better be deferred to the next meeting.—Mr. Brandreth : Does Mr. Linaker intend to retire altogether P—The Deputy Clerk : He wishes to be relieved of the duties of the Sanitary Authority.—Mr. Aaron said Mr. Linaker was a • man of great experience and ability, and he ought not to retire at the present time, when they were on the point of important negotiations with the Ship Canal Company, and they were running the risk of spending thousandsof pounds.—Deputy Clerk : He will be willing to give every assistance he possibly can.—Mr. Aaron : That's all right; but he ought to remain Clerk to the Authority until the matter is settled. Let him by all means have all the as- sistance he requires.—Mr. Mclntyre agreed with Mr. Aaron. It would be most serious to lose the services of Mr. Linaker at the present moment, arid he thought he (Mr. Linaker) ought to reconsider the matter.—The De- puty Clerk said he had told his father that the Board would wish him to reconsider the matter, and he had replied that he could not possibly reconsider it, but he would give all assistance as though he were clerk.—Mr. Heywood said they had Mr. Linaker as clerk, and the as- sistant was doing the work, and lie did not see-that they would be any better off if they settled this matter at once. He suggested that Mr. Linaker should have a little more time to consider the matter, and perhaps when he had recovered his health and spirits, his opinion would be altered.—,fr. Aaron seconded the motion, which was car- ried unanimously.

div.head: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION.
div.p: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION.

The subject of the pictorial illustration on the " Examiner" Almanac for 1891, given with this issue, is Duff House, the principal seat of the Duke of Fife, and in association with tiils principal picture are small vignettes of the Duke and his Royal wife. The portraits are excellent, and the view of the historical mansion, boldly bringing out its architectural features and surroundings, possesses high artistic merit. We hope that the picture will prove an acceptable reminiscence of a happy union. The marriage of the Princess Louise, eldest rdaughter of H.H.H. the Prince of Wales, and Alexander, sixth Duke of Fife, was celebrated on Saturday, July 27th, 1889, "with lavish pomp and. proud magnificence." The Princess Louise, who was born February 20th, 1867, had lived the quiet life of an English lady, chiefly at the old home at Sandringham. The Princess of Wales, her mother, was never happier than when with her three daughters, leading their bright, happy, even homely domestic life, and the knowledge of this fact erdeared them all the more to the heart of the nation. When the announcement of the engago- ment was made, and it was seen that out of our own Royal house in whose veins runs the blood of a long line of kings, was to be united to the Thane of : Fife, there were great rejoicings. The Right Hon. Alexander William George Duff, K.T., who was born November 10th, 1839, succeeded his father in the hereditary honours and estates on the 7th of August, 1879. lie is the sixth Earl; was educated at Eton; is a partner in the great banking firm of Sir Samuel Scott and Company; and holds many honourable offices. He is indefatigable as a pedestrian and a sportsman,and was frequently the companion of the Prince of Wales in his shooting expeditions in the Highlands. In politics he is a Liberal, and for some years represented in the house of Commons Elgin and Nairn. He is at present a Unionist. The mar- riage took place in the Buckingham Palace Chapel, in presence of the Queen,Prince and Princess of Wales, and a distinguished assembly of representatives of royal houses and ladies and gentlemen of the nobility. The return to Marlborough House was marked by great demonstrations of enthusiasm, and after the wedding breakfast, the newly-married pair were driven to their home at Upper Sheen House, up the avenue of which they passed over a carpet of wild flowers. Subsequently the Duke and Duchess went to their principal seat in Scotland—Duff House. Duff House, the picture of which we give to-day, stands within a broad domain, close by the town of Banff. It is embowered but not bidden by trees, and commands a magnificent prospect, stretching away to the blue waters of Moray Frith. The man- sion foims which has been described—a curious but still clear term—as "an oblong square." It is richly and uniformly ornamented in front and back alike, is four storeys in height,and its turrets, capi- tals, and vases stand out well, heightening the architectural effect. We are told that "two wings that were to have broadened the house, to an un- mistakeable oblong, were never added, for the liti- gious William Duff, first earl, who built the house, quarrelled with the architect, about a crack in the building, was beaten by him in alawsuit, and for a time lost all interest in the house, and lived at his seat in Rothiemay. Indeed, he went so far as to die there in 1763." The chief entrance to the house is a circular stone staircase leading to a splendid vesti- bule on the second floor. The chief rooms are large and lofty ; the library at one time ran along the whole length of the building, about 70 feet. It contains a good collection of ancient books and of Spanish literature, which it owes to the fourth earl, and the pictures are among the finest in Scotland. There is a famous full-length por- trait by Vandyck, of Frances, Duchess of Rich- mond ; a fine head of Charles 1., and por- traits of his Queen, and of Stafford, and of Lady Herbert—all by Vandyck. One of the gems of the gallery is a small picture, "The philosopher and skull," by Quintin Matsys, the blacksmith painter of Antwerp. There is a Titian, too, and several by Reynolds. In the armoury at Duff House are pre- served the great two-handled sword of the Mac- pherson-3ft. 7in. long—and three Andrea Ferraras, with a mace reported to be that of Attila, King of the Huns. The wood near the house and along the river side was for the most part p anted in 1740, when the grounds were laid out. Two trees, the Quercus oak and the Nobilis silver fir, are but young and of recent growth, for they were planted by the Prince of Wales. In the flower garden are still to be seen some remains of the famous House of Airlie, once the home of the Earls of Airlie, who then owned the estate; and some fine trees, part of the avenue which led to the old house, are still stand- ing. Through the park runs a private drive of 14 miles, and there are woody walks along the river's , edge and through the grounds. One leads on to Loch Laverock, now a beautiful rosery, but in earlier days a lake, and earlier yet mere marshland. , A mile away. overlooking the river, is the mauso- leum of the Fife family, built on the spot where stood a chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary, by Robert the Bruce. A relic of this chapel, an arched vault, with the recumbent effigy of a knight in armour, is built into the back of the mausoleum. The burial vault is underground, and contains 21 coffins, including those of the first Earl and Coun- tess, and in the mausoleum are several tablets with a rudely sculptured figure in full armour, said to be a memorial of John Duff of Muldavit, who died June 2nd, 1404. Duff House is one of the most stately of the homes of Scotland, and all, we are sure, will give willing assent to the wish that the Duke and Duchess may have long life to enjoy its comforts and the health-giving pleasures to be found in itt. picturesque surroundings. • 1

div.head: CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPL&RS.
div.p: CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPL&RS.

The monthly session of No. 1 convention of South West Lancashire, was held in the Primitive Metho- dist tabernacle, Ashton, on Saturday, when there was a full attendance of lodge deputies and repre- sentatives from Warrington, St. Helens, Widnes, Earlestown, Go'borne, Ashton, &c. The session was opened at'4 o'clock,l3ro. G. Clarke, C.C.T., of Earlestown, presiding: After the opening of the Convention, the usual Committees on credentials and reporting to the press were appointed. The reports of the Convention officers were afterwards received. The C.C.T., Bro. G. Clarke reported on the work of the lodges, and observed that public meetings had been held in various parts of the district, and that the lodges were in active work,and 1 he urgod special attention to the holding of public meet- ings. He also noted the approaching Christmas festivi- ties and recommended that lodges should as far as pos- sible hold meetings of a social character for the encour- agement and strengthening of the younger portion of the order. The report was adopted. The Convention Secretary, Bro. Sergeant T. Mantle, of Warrington, sub- mitted his report in which he particularly referred to the work among the lodges, dwelling upon the active work carried on in the shape of public meetings, special reference being made to the work of the order in War- rington. He also recomemded that a deputation be sent to Widnes to arrange for an advancement of the Order there, as he thought a visit by the Convention would act as a stimulus. The report of the Convention executive was read by the Secretary, in which mention was made of a meeting held on the previous Tuesday at St. Helens. A number of suggestions were made in the report, more particularly in reference to aggressive mis- sion works in various centres, for the purpose of strengthening one or two weak lodges, and the opening up of new ground. There were other suggestions of an interesting and practical character contained in the report, for the internal working of the order. The reports were then adopted, and arrangements were made for a visit to Widnes on the following Monday night, eight members being nominated to form a depu- tation. Ono. recommendation of the Executive, it was decided to appoint a deputation to visit the various places mentioned, where public meetings might be held, and where there was a possibility of lodges being insti- tuted. It was decided to hold the next Session at Widnes on January 10th.—The Credential Committee per Bro. Sergeant C. Price reported a total attendance of 45 representatives and officers at the Session. Bro. Morris Jones, D.C.T. of Liverpool, who arrived during the after- noon and met with a hearty welcome, gave an earnest address previous to the close of the Session. The thanks of the Convention were tended to the D.C.T.' and to the Ashton members for their arrangements, and a success- ful Session was brought to a close. A public tea was afterwards held, and was largely attended. After tea a public meeting was held in the Tabernacle Bro. G. Clark, D.C. presiding. Earnest and inspiriting addresses avere given by the Chairman, and Bro. Marris Jones D.C.T., and a programme of songs. recitations, &c., were well rendered during the evening.—Thanks to all taking part in the proceedings, closed a most encourag- ing and practical Session.

At Winchester, on Monday, James Grant, police super- intendent, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for embezzling police superannuation funds. The waiting rooms at Leigh and Bedford railway station were on Tuesday morning completely destroyed by fire, the damage being estimated at £4OO. Nine collisions, some of diem serious). were reported' in the Thames, on Tuesday, as a consequence of the fog, r and several steamers went ashore on the mud. Two more of the Lascar firemen injured by the explo- sion on board the British India Company's steamer Jumna, at the Albert Docks, died on Monday morning, making five deaths in all.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DARING SHOP ROBBERY.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named George Barker, who hails from Inkley, was charged with stealing from the shop of Thomas Din- widdie, tobacconist, Bridge-st., on Saturday afternoon, the snm of £2l 4s. in gold and silver.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner only came to Warrington on Friday, and on Saturday, from twelve to one o'clock, whilst Mr. Din- vriddie was engaged in a room behind the shop the defen- dant went in. A girl soon afterwards entered for the pur- pose of purchasing some tobacco, and she noticed the defendant leaning over the counter. As soon as defend- ant perceived the girl was watching him, he drew away from the counter, when the girl saw something in his hand, which she thought was tobacco°. The girl then stamped on the floor and called prosecutor's attention to the defendant who had then left the shop. Mr. Din- widdie at once ran out and soon overtook the prisoner, and took from him a bag which contained the amount mentioned. Prisoner was afterwards taken into custody and in answer to the charge he said, "I have nothing to say. Of course I stole it ; but if I say anything it will be worse for me." Mr. Hunt added that the prisoner was a perfect stranger, and the police were quite dependent on him for information respecting his antecedents.— Prisoner then pleaded, but said that he did not enter the shop with intent to commit felony, but merely to make a purchase. He was committed to prison for three months with hard labour.

A Paris newspaper publishes a statement in which the writer gives a detailed account of the manner in which he assisted the supposed murderer of General Seliverstoff to make his escape. The story has caused a great sensa- tion, and the authorities have decided to open an inquiry into the circumstances. Lord Stalbridge has been nominated by the directors cf the London and North-Western Railway Company as chairman, in succession to Sir Richard M oon. It is stated that Mr. George Findlay, the present general manager, will be appointed one of the new directors, and probably deputy-chairman. Cardinal Manning, writing to a correspondent on the :subject of General:Booth's " Darkest England," says the book seems to him a true and urgent appeal for the great ,multitudes of our people who are% suffering in miserable dwellings extreme poverty, and surrounded by vice and mime. If the plan was well guided they will reclaim and raise many that are now lost. Two well-dressed men entered a tramcar in Chicago, and while one stood at the door the other went among the passengers and forced them to deliver up their money and valuables. No attempt was made to arrest the rob- _kers, who got safely away with their booty.
