RUGBY.

ORFORD RANGERS T. WARRINGTON RECS.—Prayed OR the ground of the latter, on Saturday. A very rough and exciting game resulted as follows :—Recs. a tries, 3 minors; Rangers, I goal, 1 try, 2 minors. WATERLOO WHITE STAR, RUNCORN, T. FRODSHAH WHITE STAR.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, and ended in a win for the visitors by one goal and two minors to nil. T. Shallcross scored the try and Spencer kicked the goal. STOCKTON HEATH V. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND.—.This match was played at Stockton Heath on Saturday. The ground being in a very hard state two 25's were ar- ranged, and the home team losing the toss kicked off. In the first half play was of a fluctuating character, the ball travelling from one end of the field to the other very quickly. At half time the visitors had scored 3 minors from futile drops at goal to Stockton Heath nil. In the second half the home team played up with vigour, and from a scrimmage near the visitors' lines Rathbone scored for the home team. After this the visitors tried hard to equalise, but their efforts were of no avail,, and they had to retire beaten, after a hard game by Ltry to 5 minors. •

RUNCORN V. SWINTON.—This important fixture drew together a large body of spectators on the Irwell-lane ground, on Saturday. To guard against the possibility of the match being scratched owing to the severe frost which had prevailed during the week, the Committee took the precaution to protect the ground. Runcorn was represented by the following players :—Houghton, back; Jones, Crompton, and T. B. Davies, three-quarter backs; Abrams and W. Evans, half-backs; Faulkner, Hughes, Riley, Dolan, Harnpson, Gavter, Rigby, Broady, and Hancock, forwards. The Swinton team was corn. posed as follows : —Wardley, back; Murray, Valentine, and Winterbotham, three-quarters; Green and Buxton, half-backs; Paul, N. Hotchkiss, Lomas, Hall, Sharpies, Holroyd, Hallam, Walker, and Ashton (Warrington), for- wards. Play was started by Faulkner, and in a moment afterwards Davies, who received a pass from Crompton, was on his way to the visitors' goal in a determined man- ner. Eventually Davies, amid much excitement, got in under the posts. Unfortunately, although the place was an easy one, being in front of the posts, Crompton failed to augment. For some time afterwards Runcorn had the best of the play, Jones rendering every service. An at- tempt was made by Hotchkiss to break through the Run- corn men; but here Faulkner came to the rescue, and brought Hotchkiss down, and thus for the moment pre- venting what looked like danger. Swinton then became warm to the work, and Crompton making a false move, Ashton obtained a try, which was converted by Valentine. Swinton still continued to play a determined game, and Abrams averted danger. It was now the home team's turn to be doing something, and a magnificent move was made to break away. Everything looked promising; but Abrams making an attempt to kick fell, and a splendid opportunity was lost. At half-time the score :—Runcorn, one try, two minors;: Swinton, one goal. The second portion of the game was fast and determinedly fought, and Evans, having secured a try, Crompton kicked a magnificent goal. The excite- ment at this point became very great, as Runcorn in the matter of points was ahead. This position was main- tained until almost the finish of the game, when a rever- sal took place owing to Valentine dropping a goal, which was unsuccessfully appealed against. Total score—Run- corn, 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors; Swinton 2 goals, 1 minor.

FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

Lancastrians can look upon the team which has been chosen to do battle for the North against the South to- day, with more satisfaction than for many seasons. There has of late years been too preponderating a flavour of Yorkshiretnen to be palatable, but now the tables are turned, and whatever the result of the great match, Lan- cashire ought to rest satisfied with the fact that their wealth of talent has been duly recognised. The fifteen is strong at every point. Some surprise and annoyance is felt in Yorkshire at the preference of Valentine for Dyson, but in stopping rushes the stalwart Swintonian is certainly of more service than the speed fludpi‘....c-- tnree-quarter. The latter, it is will- ,—is on the re- serve, but unless sickness spTh he is not likely to be called upon. fler.s- -hopes to be all right for the match, but he can scarcely be as fit and well as one would de- sire.

A large number of Rugby players were thrown idle on Saturday afternoon. Many of the grounds which had been left unprotected were frozen so hard that play was altogether out of the question. Hence such engagements as Manchester v. Free Wanderers, Manchester Rangers v. Warrington, Leigh v. Wigan, Rochdale Hornets v. Liverpool Old Boys, Oldham v. Batley, dm., had to be postponed.

Broughton Rangers came in for rather severe treat- ment at St. Helens, where the Recreation had the better of them by a couple of goals and three tries to a goal. Pilkington and Parr were very conspicuous for the "Glassblowers," both scoring twice, and as a rule the Rangers were hard put to it. St. Helens were also suc- cessful, pulling off their game at Tyldesley by a try only. A good deal of the time was spent in hunting for the ball amongst the straw, with which the field had been pro- tected.

Swinton may be said to have been fortunate at Run- corn, the verdict being in their favour by two goals (one dropped by Valentine) to a goal and a try. Davies ran in only a minute after start, but Crompton failed in the place-kick, although it was in front of the posts.

div.head: Ai3BOCIATION.
div.p: Ai3BOCIATION.

The draw for F. A. Cup was productive of more than one sensation, First and foremost must be placed Sunderland v. Everton. It seems a pity that one of these two powerful clubs must go to the wall so early in the competition. The same teams meet at Sunderland in a League fixture to-day, and it is sure to attract a vast amount of attention. Accrington v. Bolton Wanderers is another instance of two League members falling foul of each other. The Reds will have the advantage of ground, but the Wanderers will make a tremendous bid for victory. Preston North End may also find a hard task at Stoke, where the home team are sure to struggle to the very last.

The rest of the big clubs are fairly favourably drawn, but it must not be imagined that the present holders 0 the cup (Blackburn Rovers) will have a walk over at Middlesbrough. Notts Forest are *drawn with a London club for the third season in succession. The Reds are very likely to run well up in the ties, if thP draws do not go dead against them. They are a very fine team.

Of the League matches that were down for decision on Saturday last, two were interfered with by frost and fog, but the other four were brought to a satisfactory conclu- sion. Everton were much too smart for Derby County, and are consequently still at the head of the table. Wyllie, one of the new Everton forwards, made his presence felt, and INl'Lean was again a worthy substitute for Doyle. The great Liverpool club have a splendid goal record— far in advance of any of their rivals. Wolverhampton Wanderers created some astonishment by beating the Albion at West Bromwich, more especially as Groves- appeared with the latter for the first time. It was a desperate game all through, the only goal:being scored by the Wolves directly before play ce.a-sed.

Bolton Wanderers were visited by Accrington and ran clean away from them. Football could hardly be said to be safe, the hard turf lying under the thin coating of snow,but although the players slipped about a good deal, no one was injured. The home forwards were tar and away smarter than their opponents and beat them by six goals to none. Hay was hardly seen at his best between the posts, but he had plenty of occupation. The Rovers journeyed to Birmingham, where they drew with the Villa, who the week prevbus were sadly overplayed at Blackburn. Townley came out better than at any time this season, and both John Southworth anel Lofthouse put in good work. Brandon was missing from the ranks of the visitors, Douglas turning out with his old com- rades once more.

div.head: LECTURE BY MR. LEADER WILLIAMS.
div.p: LECTURE BY MR. LEADER WILLIAMS.

At stre Albert-st. Schools, Altrincham, on Monday night,. Mr. E. Leader Williams, engineer to the Manchester Ship Canal, gave a history on the great underta-king. The Rev. E. 3- Trevitt presided. Mr. Williams said the Manchester Ship Canal was a work which was the outcome otf a series of long investigations in l'arliamentary Committees in the yeare, of 18834-5. its supporters spent' £150,00 in obtaining the Act. The object of the promoters was, to cheapen the cost of carriage by bringing large steamers and other vessels from the sea to Manchester, avoiding the heavy landing and carting charges at Liverpool, and reducing by one- half, the railway and dock rates.. This was insured by the adoption of dock dues at Manchester and rates on the Ship. Canal.. which were fixed by the Act of Parliament at onek-half the rates and dues charged on.the various descriptions of traffic using the Liverpool docks and the railways to Man- chester.. Having described the original plan, Mr. Williams gave a generaVoutline of the engineer- ing plans, and showed that the group of locks at Eastham would admit of at very large amount of shipping every tide, more-particularly as on all tides above the ordinary, level of the canal, all the lock gates would beopen /or a considerable period before high water. Spring tides would rise five to seven feet above the ordinary levet of the tidal portion of the canal, which extends to the next group of locks at Latchford, a distance of 21 miles. The total length of the canal is 35-li miles. From Latchford to Manchester (a distance of 141 miles) the canal will be filled with the waters of the Mersey, Irwell, and other rivers. The canal being designed to take the place of the rivers Irwell and Mersey from Man- chester to Latchford, it will thus become a canalized river, continuing to be the mairudrain for Lancashire and Cheshire, large sluices being provided at each set of locks-to deal with land floods and surplus water. Owing to the sewage of Manchester, Sal- ford, and all the other towns on the. rivers Irwell and Mersey and their tributaries being allowed to flow into the rivers without purification, the state of the water-has become very bad. Salford has now completed a-system of interceptilw sewers, and is about to purify the sewage-at works constructed Pt Mode Wheel. Somewhat similar works are now being constructed by Manchester, and as the turn- ing of crude sewage into rivers or streams is con- trary to the law as well as injurious to health, the other towns above Manchester must take• immedi- ate steps to prevent their sewage polluting the canal. Some of them have now got this necessary work in hand. Referring to the pollution of the Irwell and Mersey, Mr. Williams expressed his pleasure at the action taken' by the County Councils of Lancashire, Cheshire and Derbyshire, to put the River/Pollution Act into force. At present it was no use for a man to go fishing in. the Irwell. (Laugh- ter.) There were no fish, but there were dead dog fish, and no good to anyone.. (Renewed laughter.) In the tidal portion of the canal between Eastham and Latchford, 12 ' miles are inland,,and nine miles on the foreshore or bed, of the tideway ;. on this portion em- bankments have to be formed. Where the foundation is rock or clay they are formed of clay hearting pro- tected by heavy stonework. In, some cases, where the bases of the embankment are on sand, close piling is driven on each side of the foot of the embankments. At Runcorn, where the Mersey is not so wide as lower down the river, instead of an embankment, a concrete wall is being constructed. le addition to, the locks and sluices at Eastham to allow, of the flow of the tide into and out of the estuary portion of the canal, when the tide rises above the ordinary water level,, three weirs, each 600 feet long, are to be constructed in the embankments. In the embankment opposite the River Weaver, 10 large sluices, each 30 feet wide, have been built to allow of the passage of the Weaver water out of the canal. These sluices will also be used for tidal dew. After sketching the general features of the cutely Mr. Williams said the canal was being excavated throughout its whole lenr to a minimum width of 120'feet at the ' averaged 172 feet -

TEM INFIRMARY AND PAUPER PATIENTS. The Worts:um:7BE MASTER (Mr. Ward) reported that a man named Robert Murray had been admitted suffering from a fractured leg. Mnrray had been discharged frbm the Infirmary;;but seemed to be unable to walk, fcr- he fell down whilst OD his way to the Workhouse. De' had £3 12s. and a silver watch in his possession.—The CHAIRMAN: BOST did the man come from the Infirmary'? --The Won L-onst.. 'Vas ruu said the man tried to walk but he fell down on the bridge. Several men had been sent in the same way. This man was a chair-mender and came from Derbyshire.—The CHAIRMAN thought it would be really more humane if a relieving offiner was communicated with before a man was turned out of the linfannary in this way.—Mr. Ilekrow-caid this was not the first case of the kind, and if the statements that were made were true they reflected no credit on the, Infirmary.—Mr. Hooo,Wnionr, said that if the man- had between £3 and £V-irk his pocket it could not be said that he was destitute.—Mr. BEATON said that if the man was not destitute it would have been more reasonable to send for a cab than to send him out into, the street.—The CHATIDIAN remarked that if the relieving officer had been sent Jot., there would have been no danger to the man. He (the Chair, man) would, however, see the medical man at the Infit-- mar', in regard to the case.—Mr. Oman said-the Board could not dictate to the Infirmary.—Mr. JifLLBYI Why should we give £lO a year towards the Infirmary ?-,-The CLERK pointed' out that the man had in his pocket £3 10s., and they could hardly expect the Infirmary people to look upon, him as a pauper.—The CHAIRMEeN cpses-i tioned whether they would know the- man had anyil money or not.—Mr. JOLLEY said there had been a pauper., case of the same kind.—The subject then dropped.' The Board then resolved into a Committee meeting.to consider the applications for the post of chaplain to t` Workhouse.

tu .ne upper Manchester oarcnir o lanchester would be 170 feet wide at the bottom, and 230,feet at water level. At the various locks the canal was widened out considerably,and would admit of vessels turning, The width adopted would allow of large steamers passing each other at any part of the canal and where works were built on the sides of the canal for manufacturing purposes the canal would be widened out to allow of shipping lying alongside wharves without interfering with the passage of vessels Imp and down the canal. Having described the works At Latchford and Barton, Mr. Williams explained 'how the existing railways would be carried over :the canal by means of great bridges. The docks at Manchester will have an area of water space of 114 acres, the area of quay space being 152 acres. The length of quays will be similes At Warrington a dock is proposed to be constructed of an area of 23 acres. At Partington the canal is widened out to allow steamers to lie on either side, and branch railways will be constructed with hydraulic coal tips to enable either Lancashire or Yorkshire coals to be expeditiously loaded into shipping. o. The various-railway companies are about to construct branches to the Manchester docks in order to enable them to compete with the extensive system of inland canals which are joined to the Ship Canal. One of the most important of these canals, that known as the Bridgewater Canal, with its branch canals and the docks at Runcorn, has been purchased by the Ship Canal Com- pany. With the use of the electric light, steamers will be able to navigate by night as well as by day, and the whole length of the canal will be traversed in about ten hours. As to the contention that they could not get sufficient water for the canal, he thought that the ques- tion had been settled forever for they filled the canal on one Sunday morning. (Laughter and applause.) It filled rather more quickly than they wanted, and it kept him from church, and wet him through. (Laughter.) At all events the question was settled for ever. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Williams described the sources of the water supply, and showed that from the enormous watershed of Lancashire, Cheshire, and Derbyshire they could with the greatest ease, have what was really a canalized river. The problem was, would the water flowing down, the Irwell and the Mersey be sufficient for the lockage? Mr. Williams explained the scheme of pounds, locks, and sluices, and said the question was as to the amount of water going over the weir at Throstle's Nest. This had been very accurately calculated, and he (Mr. Williams)o had proved that there was enough water flowing to put seventy large ships a day through the locks. Seeing that there were not more than thirty a day going, into Liver-- pool, their supply' was quite large enough. The length of the canal from Stickings to Irlam was 311 miles, andit contained two very wide parts, where the locks were being built, at Barton and Irlam. The pumps which had been, put in had lowered the canal at the rate of 2 feet 6 inchesa day. That was pretty good pumping, (Hear, hear.) If they could do this, they would be able to pump any quantityof water that might be required by the Ship Canal. For the excavation nearly 100 steam excavators- of various types have been employed, some of which have been constructed in France and Germany. To convey the earth to the spoil grounds, and for other purposes,, L 73 locomotives and 6,300 wagons and trucks are now employed, 223 miles of railway having bovan, laid alongside or in the bed of the canal. The rate of exca— vation has varied from to 1 million cubic yards per month. As much as 2,400 cubic yards have been exca— vated in ten hours by the German excavators ; but:di-41'r average would be less than 2,000 cubic yards. The, deepest cutting is near Runcorn, where, for a.short die.- tance,.the depth is 66 feet. The largest cutting is, ate Latchford, where, for a distance of 14 miles, the depth. averages 55 feet. The slopes of the cutting vary with the nature of the soil from, I'. to. 1 to 2' to one_ In the rock cuttings the sides are nearly vertical. The total amount of ea, cavation in the canal and docks ainounhi, to, about 46;000,000 cubic yards, 10,000,000 i cubic yards. of which is sandstone rock. The spoil from the canal.) is used in filling up the river bends, which are cut.-offb3r the canal , and in raising the low-lying lands near to„so as to-make them available for being used for shin-build- log and other purposes. The advantage which, manu- facturers will enjoy alongside a great wateway connected by railway and canal with thaxvhole oE the manufactur- ing and other districts in the northern and midland counties of England will, it is confidently expeotecl„ltead to largeindustries being established on the banks. cit the canal, which will develop much trade.,independentiv of the through traffic to and' from the. sea from, the Man- chester Docks. The canal. from Warrington to Manches- ter being free from tidal influence, the water level will be always the same, and lay-byes, 073 side, docks, can be cheaply constructed at any point, as gate en- trances will not be required. The coal and salt fields of Lancashire and Cheshire are near the canal, and con- nected with it by rail and waterways. The chemical works of St. Helens, Widnes,. and Runcorn as well as the coal, iron, and pottery trades of Staffordshire, have the same advantages. Thew industries, with the great manufacturing districts o Lancashire and Yorkshire, will secure a large trade to the canal, which will deal with the largest population and trade ever established in a similar area, (Applause.) At the close Mr. Williams took part in a general con— versation on the work of the canal, in which he diffused, a large amount of intsresting information. He showed. how the old canal of the Bridgewater Navigation Co., which had been purchased by the Ship Canal Conapany, for £.1,710,000 was still paying as well as ever it did„ even against all the competition of the railways.. Mr. Williams incidentally observed that he had all his own savings invested in the canal, and he had every can- fldence in its future. A hearty vote of tharks was accorded, to Mr. Williams for his lecture,

TILE EARLESTOWN TRAGEDY.

-- TRIAL AT TH.E ASSIZES. Arthe Crown Court at St. George's RaII, Liverpool, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Cave Thomas Mtrcer, (29),,. labourer, was indicted with that he did, at the township of Newton, on the 115th July, feloniously, wil. fully,,and of his malice aforethought, kill and murder , one Thomas Kay. Mr. Cunningham and Mr. Tobin were for the Crown, and Mr. Swift defended. Upon the'pri- soneriaeieg called.tipon to plead he stood for some time speechless, the muscles of his fhee twitching convulsively. As heoppeared not to understand the words which had been addressed to him, the chief warder repeated them, and then •he said in a low tone " Guilty, ' and upon the question being repeated he returned the tame answer,

Mr. Swift said his lordship would remember that when the prisoner was asked to p:bad to the indictment ten; days ago, he said precisely the same thing. He (the counsel) then pleaded that the prisoner could not pos- sibly plead guilty to a charge of murder. His abrdship : Yes. I think it must be taken as a plea of not ;guilty. Mr... Swift said he hoped lthat Dr. Barr would have, ; been in court for he wanted to ask him a question—his , lordship would know what he meant—before- the pri- soner was charged, Dr. Barr had been suspended by the 1 prosecution, and had notice to be there. A plea Of not guilty was entered by the Clerk of. AiTailePa.

Micreottingham, in his opening statement, said the prisonerhad previously been employed in the neighbour- hood of Earlestowti, but some time ago it had been supposed that a sum of money was coming to him and the rest of his family from his grandfather,and although he was working at that time, no sooner did he hear of that money than he worked no more. Since that time he had teen steeping out, and getting scarcely any work, subsisting on the charity of 'friends. It did not appear that the two men had any bad feelings between them, hut there was no doubt that key came to'his death by the.violence of the prisoner.. .On the 23rd July the deceased was working at the old paper mills,Earlestown, chipping bricks, and for that purpose he had-borrowed an azo, from one Thomas Hatton. This was found by ,himiaiot to be very convenient, however, and he ,got another axe, keeping the other by him. Ow the 26th july the prisoner, between ten and eleven o'clock-in the morning,, was seen talking to the deceased man, who , was at work there with the double-headed axe besides him. At 'that time they appeared to be on friendly! terms*, but a short time afterwards a carter named Singleton, who was at work about twenty yards away,, heard a cry, and turning round saw the prisoner stand- ing. behind Kay in the act of striking him on the head, ' with the double-headed axe. The prisoner afterwards , ran away up a passage to a place called Vitriol Kay' NVRS picked up, and taken to the office. of the works,- where it was found her was unconscious, and, was bleeding from wounds on the head. Some time afterwards prisoner was takem, as he lay near the, .Vitrcl Hill to the office and was shown Kay as he lay I unconscious. When he was charged, he said, ." He .brought it on himself. I told him I was going to ask for some work, and he said what right had a fellow like me knocking about so long to expect-i. get work.". That was the only excuse the prisoner had for inflicting the wounds on the head. The deceased died on the,. 31st August. The counsel, in conclusion, ,contended that so long as the prisoner had suffiiiient mind left to distin- guish between right and wrong, and to resist the impulse to do wrong, he was responsible for his actions. John Hatton deposed to lending the deceased an axe. Mr. Swift : He could not say whether the prisoner weneur his right mind. He had not seen him fertile last three or four years, but he believed he was generally. .calledthe gold seeker. Thbmas Newton, an employ-'at-the Old Paper - identified two chipping axes produced as those used by -thedeceased on the date named. Thomas Singleton, carter, said that on the 26th .J 1.113 he-was carting bricks from the Old Paper. Mills. Hear- rived- at about a quarter to eleven. Kay was chipping bricks, and the prisoner was beside him, They- were talking apparently in a friendly manner. While loading his cart, witness heard someone shouting "Oh V", Tam- ing round, lhe saw the prisoner striking Kay on the head with an axe. Witness ran for help, and on coming, back he saw the prisoner running away, and Kay lying bleed- ing Munco,A William Moses, joiner, Earlestown, said he li-E—ad c -oftheoworkmen in Mr. Kellett's employment. He-had seen the prisoner about the works frequently before-the murder. On the 26th July, in the forenoon he saw-the. prisoner running away towards Vitriol Mound.- John O'Neill, in the employment of Mr. Kellett, stated , that shortly after eleven on the 28th July, on being told: .something, he went towards the Vitriol Mound and found the prisoner lying among some thistles. He ape peared to have been sleeoing, sad when awakened by -witness, he said, " WhatT to do ?" Witness said, "1 ,willlet you know what's to do." , Police-constable Hughes„stationed at Netvtons,aid that en the 26th July he went to the paper works, where he found deceased being carried into Mr. Moses' Office. He -went to the place where 10,ty had been working. He there i found an axe wet with blood and clotted with hair. .Tbaire was a pool of blood at the place, Htl.afterwartts received at the office a felt hat, having a cut in it. lie took the prisoner into custody. There was a spat oft:lend .On his right cheek. He charged the prisoner, and he re- plied, "It was his own fault I did it. I was geingto ask ,Kitl.lett for a job this morning, and ,he said., thing like you to ask RR a job, that has been knocking about so long ?" After Kay's death he. again charged prisoner with the murder, and he replied i". Did: he. die this afternoon ?"

Pe. Valentine, Earle ' tiown said he had been • calledi to see• Kay at the eld paper million the 26th Jilyc Elb-was totally unconscious. Els had on the head fire • wounds, and there was also a complicated fracture of the shrill, nd he directed his removal to the Infirmary. Ernest Edward Bowden, junior head surgeon at War- rington Infirmary, said Kay was admitted on the-28th Jy and remained unconscious till his death-, , Police-sergeant Lcuigworth said that when • they were about to remove the•prisoner to the cells the prisoner said, ‘4 I only hit him on the head with the hatchet- once, and -threw it at him." Ile had noticed that the prisoner was Not so sharp as othoi people, but still he thoughtheknew right from wrong. Dr. Joseph Wiglnsworth, merlicaL superintendent at Rainhill Asylum, said that in October last he.hadais inter- view with prisoner, and conversed with hina•some time. ; So far as he could Pdge the prisoner, was a man of weak intellect, but not absolutely insane.. He was capable of conversing rationally, and had an appreciatitz of things !• •in general. but not a thorough appreeiatioru For in- stance, he 'clearlyrunderstood that the act wasan ulawful ; one but he did net seem to believe that -the inlaries he had given were•sufficient to causo,dentla. Cross-examined by Mr. Swift„ witness-said he con- eidered that theeprisoner had been all his life a person of weak intellect, ills mental condition approximating rather to imbecility than insanity-. The intellectual powers were below the average, and he seemed to have less capa- city for contreLaf his passions than ordinary persons, and not the same appreciation of his acts.

Dr. Barr,oni.b:eing examined by Mr. Tobin, said the prisoner had been under his cbservation, since the 12th August last: He had frequent- conversations with him, and looked upon him as a man of weakintellfect,of stupid and passiOnate temperament He also. suffered from deafness, ydlich increased hif3-,stupidity: At the time of his reception in prison he appeared tn-beitak half starved, state. The conclusion witness. came to. was that not., only wa..ithe prisoner's Mind weak,,but-was wholly une- cultivated. The prisoner seemed todenovr the act he didl was wrong,, but he did not seem .teAttachtnuch tance to that act. The prisoner seemed to have come ta the conclusion that he had already beam tried, and that' It was time he was dischr-rged fromprison. By.the,Judge : The prisoner seemed to think that the • triabefOre the magistrates.was hiS•tvial. Cress-examined, witness said ke• thought the condAion of mental weakness described hadi emisted all priscset's. life. He thought these-causes.eomttined would prevent, him from fully appreciating the•neaure of his act. He. evidently did not fully appreciete•Ose nature of the act be was committing. He thought he had received very. r great provocation, and that the, enjury he inflicted; WS. net in excess of the prevocatibm. ' Mo. Swift, on behalf of thesprisainer, pointed out,thelz the fact that the charge of manslaughter was includtedi , the indicitment as well as.the charge of murder, PR) did not suppose the.jery Nitould on the hearinn, of the evielence accuse the mama arnv such object and motive as would involve him, io the crime of willul murder. Having regard to.all the, circumstances of the caseand p.ntting them together and regarding them in the light of the very weak intellect of the prisoner, he thought- they 'would come to the conclusion that at the very- most the crime was manslaughter, though thn act might be murder. The Judge, in, surnaming up, said that had this man been of ordinary intellect he should undoubtedly have told them that they would not have to find a ver- dict of murclor. The &fence was that the man was not a man ordinary intellect, and there weretwo courses open to them according as the circumstances were deemed to be made out or not. They might come to the conclusion: that the man wasinsane. at the time, and consequently was entitled to be acvitted, or they might come to the conclusion the,'a although not insane at the time, he was in such a mental condition that he ' did not fully understand what- he was doing. Un- doubtedly an insane man was not responsible for his actions. To, be satisfied, however, that a man was in- sane„ it mustbe proved, either that he did net know what he was doing or that what he was doing Was wren... The testimony, however„ went to show that he knew that what he was doing was wrong. This cues- ton might be put aside, but then came the case which , related topeople partially insane. His running away, land when arrested giving an excuse for the act he had ;committed showed that he knew that he was doing wroag. The jury at once found a verdict of manslaughter, His Lordship said that as it was a very peculiar case he Would defer sentence till this morning to consider what he would do.

for sentence at the Assizes,Cat Bt. George's Hall. His Lordship said the prisoner had been shown to be a. • person of defective intellect. He was clearly not insane • and it would have been a cruelty to haw acquitted . him.upon that ground, which would have resulted in • his being locked up in a criminal lunatic asylum for the. resit of his life. The znedical evidence satisfied him that the prisoner was not insane to that extent but somewhat detclent in intellect. Unfortonately, he was of a pea. - sihrtate nature, and not of that class of persons who were considere4 harmless ; but with the absence to • some extent of reasoning powers, having a tem- , perament which made him a very dangerous person He had shown a reckless disregard of human life. aud suffering, and from his tendency to take an exag- gerated view of what was done in the way of provocation he showed that he was not fit to be ' at • large without danger to his fellow-creatures. He must, thereforsipa.ss upend:line a sentence of penal servitude of some duration. At thesame time, if he showed during the period of its • proessthat he might be let out without further danger to his fellow-creatures he would recommend in the proper- - quartir some remission of that sentence. -The .septance was one of fifteen years' penal servitude.

SOLICITOR. . Fairly on Friday morning birl.Thomas Dyson, who resides at Prescot, fell off the platform at Limcan: . Railway Station, and was ram over by an incoming_ train.. When taken up it was found that one of his legs was severely fractureeosnd he was removed in the ambulance carriage to the Northern Hospital,. where he died shortly before six o'clock. Deceased,.. whrewan a solicitor of Present, WWl' a son of Mr: Etheard ,Dytien, formerly of St. Helens gasworks. He was agedabont 33, and was unmarried. The news of Abe death of Mr. Dyson, occasioned a painful, feeling in Prescot and St. Helens. Though his residence and offices were in Church-st., Prescot, he was well-known in St. Helens, and frequently appeared as an advocate at the sittings of the county court. He served his, articles with. .a, firm of solicitors at Peterborough, and commenced nractice on his own account at Present about :five years. ..ago i The deceased gentleman's father was formerly. .secretary of the Corporation Gas Works at St. Helens.—. .2i/ft:Clarke Aspinall held an inquest at Liverpool, on ,Saturday, on the body of the deceased gentleman.. Dd..- , dence was given that deceased was found lying in the Ifour foot between the platform and Edge-hill tunnel. ,The railway company were unable to produce any --evi- dence as to how the deceased came to be in the fourfoot. .He had been at the Assizes in the afternoon, and was . last seen by a friend about six o'clock on Tharsday .evening. Mr. W. Mackenzie, Prescot, appeared , on-be- half of the deceased's relatives, while the London. and Ntirth-Western Railway Company were repiisented by tdr. W. J. Bland. The)ury returned an open verdict. . The remains of the late Mr. Dyson, were interred in the -burial ground attached to Present parish church on Tues- day afternoon. The officiating clergyman wastheNicar,. the Rev. H. Mitchell. A large number of gentlemen attended, including solicitors, members of tho,Prescot.. Cfinservative Club, of which deceased was a committee- man, and Oddfellows, in connection with which- order the late Mr. Dyson was P.G..M. of the Earl Derby,Ledge, Arr. Webster, assistant organist, rendered, the " Dead aarch " and other selections as the mournera were. entering and leaving the church. The cofffitwas covered : with handsome floral contributions. • Not the least taken aback at the result,of lecture outhe question of the Depots, last sweet, ~,Mr. Diggle appeared at the. Borough Court, on Mon- , day; and, after the ordinary business had been • , posed of, he placed in the hands of the Mayor ter which he had received from Alderman WI which he requested should he-read aloud. The DI , Complied with this request, and the letter worded as follows:—" , have only just seen plans for the abating of the nuisance at the Depbb morning, or I weeld have laid them before the Sat • Committee last night. If it meats with your appto, will place the plans in the hands of the Borough Sur with instructionsato report upon the same to the ing on Wednesday night. I shall be very pleas your scheme provez a success.--,Teser En. Wnronr."- Mayor: That is all you want is it net ; you desire the Se.ni., tary Committee to ;gave you a proper hearing?-Mr. Higgle answered in the affirmative, and suggested that his worship should occupy the chair at the Committee meeting. He wished to have a fair hearing, far the inhabitants ,of the town wanted to know something about the matter.—The Mayor : It looks as though your plans are going to be submitted before the Sanitary Com- mittee, and that is exactly what you desire.—Mr. Diggle: It is, and if you will Attend as chairman, I shall be very much pleased. -,'Fbe 'Mayor : You know that there is a man much greater than me on that Committee.—Mr. Diggle : Ah !I will snake him mach less. (Laughter.')-- The Mayor: I will see what Alderman Burgess says.—Mr. Diggle: Be lathe oalyunan in the town that I am afraid of.—The Mayor: If you can prove to Alderman Burgess : that your plans are good and workable, the Committee .will be too glad to approve of the4l.--41ere Mr. Diggle banded up another letter from Mr. Longdin which read, •" I should be glad to seethe plans so that I can report + . upon them."—The Mayos said it was quite evident that Mr. Diggle was going to have his scbemeahrought to the; , front n0w...,--Llderman Sutton, addressing Mr. Diggle, , said, he thought the Committee had always told him that I they would be very glad to do anything ,• to abate, tbe , nuisance. He had no doubt but that be Committee, would give the plans every consideration. and deal with them According to the manner they thought fit.—Mr. Diggle then lamented the file that he was not on the ,Sanitary Committee, and expressed his desire to be put on, but this, he said, he could only attain by the proper -course.—Alderman Harrison (ocularly to the Mayor) : We can snake him en Alderman, and by that means he might be selected to serve on the Committee.—Alder- man Sutton said it was a pity Mr. Diggle could not per- suade the inhabitants of the borough that he was so Diggle: I do not want to persuade them.— The subject then dropped, and Mr. Diggle left the Court, full of smiles' which are his characteristic under .almost any circumstances,

• WAERINGTON SAy [GS BANK,;
ANNUL MEETING.

- - The annual meeting of the trustees and managers of the Warrington Savings Bank was held at the Bank premises, on Tuesday !morning. Major Pick- mere presided, and there were also present Mr. W. Long (vice-chairman), the Mayor, (Alderman Fran- 'comb), Aldermen Holmes, Davies, ,and Harrison Rev. J. Yonge, Rev.F. LFreestofl, and Rev. E. ' Moore; Councillors ineming, Blackhurst, H. Ro- berts, and F. W. Monks; Major Litton, Messrs. P. Monks, J. R. Young, W. Derbyshire, R. Garnett, J. White, G. Dakin, and J. E. Davies (actuary). REPORT AND ATATIOARNT OE 'ACCOIDMS. The ACTUARY read the report of the Committee of Tianagement which stated that the total funds amounted to £297,609 113 s. 9d. as under: With the National Debt Commissioner on genera account, £293,195 10s. 5d., on separate surplus fund account, carrying interest, £1,200, on separate surplus fund account not carrying Interest, £7,000, and with Mr. J. C. Parr, treasurer, 122,514 4d., making a total of A 297,609 Hs. 9d. The total amount due to depositors wa.s £294,774 7a. Bd., leaving a surplusof £2,835 us. Id. The above plainly showed to depositors that the Government had in hand more than would pay the amount due to them, and that with the amount in the treasurer's hands there was the large surplus of £2,835 I.ls. Id. There bad been an increase of 223 accounts in the year and the total number of depositors was now 10,562. The business of the bank steadily inereased,the number of transactions during the par being 17,666 as against 16,571. in 1889 and 14,600 in the year MO. The report waseigned on behalf of the Committee of Management' by Major Pickmere (chairman) and Mr. Long (vice-chairman), The state. meet of accounts was also submitted. - The CitautarAia, in moving that the statement of accounts be approved, said that, looking to the fact that Warrington was so well favoured with sound undertak- ings in which investors might place money with confid- ence—perhaps better so than most towns—it was grati- fying that their committee could present so favourable a report. That savings tank was, cf course, intended for small investors, and it was natural that some depositors. when they reached the maximum, would withdraw and invest elsewhere, or they might continue depositing their savings there. It was one of the objects of the institu- tion to persuade people to make a start in saving, and there were, no doubt, many who could look back with pleasure to their young days when they brought their eavings there and who had since lived provident lives and become independent in their old age. No better ad- vice could be given to the young than to become inves- tors, and parents should permit their children to become depositors and encourage them in every way to be proud of their bank books by letting them to attend at the bank themselves and deposit their sav- ings. They might depend upon it that most of those young depositors would bless the day they first attended there and acquired the habit of laying some- thing by for a rainy day, and those good people who advised them to save and saw the happy results, would never regret the day they gave the advice, (Hear, hear.) ' Referring to the increas3 of business at the bank, the Chairman mentioned that in 1880, when he was first appointed Chairman, the number of depositors was 8,655. and the number of transactions, 14,600. This veer the number of depositors was 10,562 and they had had 17,666 transactions. (Hear, hear.) Major LITTON having teconded the proposed adoption of the statement of accounts, it was agreed to. On the motion of Mr. J. WRITE, seconded by Coun- cillor H. ROBERTS, the report of the Committee of Man- agement was adopted, and the Committee were thanked for their valuable services. ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN', &C. On the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by the Rev. J. YONGE, Major Pickniere was re-elected chairman, and Mr. W. Long vice-chairman. Councillor FLEMING moved that the following gentle- men be requested to form a committee of management: —The Chairman and vice-Chairman, Rev. J. Yonge, Major Litton, Alderman Francomb, Alderman Sutton, Mr. F. Monks, Alderman Holmes, Mr. R. Garnett, Alder- man Davies, Mr. W. Darbyshire, Alderman Harrison, and Mr. J. R. Young. On the suggestion of the Rev. J. Yonge, the Rev. F. S. Freeston's name was added to the list, which was then adopted. On the proposition of Alderman Davies the following names were added to the list of trustees: the Rev. J. Yonge, Alderman Chandley, Alderman Harrison, Mr. W. D. Houghton, and Alderman Francomb.

THE LATE XII. S. MGM The CrteutmeN moved a resolution, expressing the sin- cere condolence of the trustees and managers of the bank with the widow of the late Mr. S. Rigby, who had for many years been a trustee, and who had acted as chair- man of the bank. He (the Chairman) was away from home when the death of Mr. Rigby took place, and it was a very great shock indeed to him when he read of it in the papers. He did not think a kinder man than Mr. Rigby ever lived. He was good-hearted, generous, and of a fine genial disposition, and personally, he might al- most say, he would never meet his like again. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. Low), in seconding the proposal, said Mr. Rigby was equally kind and equally anxious to do the beet he could for everything he had in hand and every- body with whom he was connected. The motion was then agreed to.

SUGGESTIONS. Mr. R. GARNETT suggested that in addition to the £2 10s. per cent. given at the bank they might give, in order to encourage depositors, and especially the young ones, a bonus on deposits up to say, £lO or £2O. The Acrus.ny said the Government would net allow them to give anything nuctse than the 24 per cent.—Mr. GARisierr could not see the good of accumulating money.—The CRAIRmax : We may want a new bank soon.—Mr. Gan- liETT thought something should be done to popularise the institution. Be had sugaested that a prize of £lO or £2O should be given for an eGsay which could afterwards be printed and distributed.—The Cirernmaar said theywere not like a public company, as. they had hard and fast lines laid down for them. The Commissioners ,for the Reduction of the National Debt would not allow them to put that £lO or £2O down as expenses to•the bank, and they should have to find it out' of their own pockets.— The ACTUARY said he couldniake inquiries as to that mat- ter, and the discussion then dropped. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close. •

EXTRA ORDINARY FATALITIES ON A
SCROONER AT WESTON POINT.

This week the schooner Lady N9ave, of Beau- mans, arrived at Weston Point with a cargo of flints from Dieppe. The Captain,lsaac Jones, reports that while lying in Dieppe Harbour on the 23rd November, an able seaman named Thomas Roberts. a nephew of the master, and Owen Jones, the cook, were suffocated in the forecastle. It appears that when the mate went to call the cook at 7 a.m. to prepare breakfast, he found the forecastle on fire, and calling the Captain they descended into the place. The atmosphere was so charged with fumes and smoke that all efforts to light a candle by means of matches were of no avail. The Captain ascended the ladder, and on returning with a light, the two men had been suffocated. Roberts was at the foot of the stairs, partly undressed, and Jones was lying in his bunk. The explanation is that the mut who were the only occupants of the forecastle, on going, to bed left burning a paraffin lamp, which was hung on a post about six inches from the deck, which was set on fire, and burned entirely through in one part. Although the hatchway was open; the fumes had proved sufficient to suffocate the occupants of the place. The lamp had apparently been extinguished by its own fumes as it was out when the unfortunate men were discovered. Roberts was 18 years of age, and a native of Manchester, while Jones was aged 17 years, and was a native of Amloch.

div.head: Letter to the Obttor.
div.p: Letter to the Obttor.

WATERLOO BRIDGE AND ITS APPROACHES, &c. Sir,—Standing on Waterloo Bridge this afternoon, I was much struck with the very slow progress which is being made towards the completion of the alterations which were sanctioned by the Commissioners a long time ago, and I began to soliloquize, and wonder if some of us were to fall asleep like Rip Van Winkle,we should not, on our awakening,still find the bridge with its approaches in an unfinished state. Slowness of movement seems to be a characteristic of our governing body except where their action takes the form of increasing emoluments of our public servants, in which case they " facilitate the expenses." The work should be pushed on more rapidly. All the heavy traffic passes over this bridge both to and from the station, and the delay in its completion must cause serious inconvenience to carting operations, bosides mak- ing the road unsafe for pedestrians, it being the leading thoroughfare from the busiest and most important part of the town. The Commissioners have it in their power to forward the work by taking in hand and completing ' the road, so far as practicable, on either side of the bridge, and also making the alterations for which pur- pose the coal yard and house at the corner of Waterloo- rd. and High-st., were purchased. If the Commissioners did not intend to pull down the house for so long a time after it became the property of the town, why, in the name of common sense, did they not re-let it when the tenant's notice was up, and so give the ratepayers the benefit of the rent instead of allowing it to remain empty doing nothing. When will our rulers rise to a sense of their duty ? The granolithic pavement recently laid in Greenway Road has shewn signs of giv- ing way,but then what else could have been anticipated, seeing that it was put down too late in the year, unless the Commissioner thought Providence would come to their aid and withold the frost for a season. If the Board had not been so tardy in making up their minds as to the kind of pavement they intended to lay, this would not have happened, as sufficient time would have elapsed to have allowed the granolithic to thoroughly set and the moisture to evaporate before the frost came. lam sorry for the consequence, because it laid under proper condi- tions (though not so durable as flags) it makes a clean and substantial footway. Yours truly, RESIDENT. Runcorn, 11th Dec., 1890.

div.head: COMMON SENSE V. RECONCILEMENT.
div.p: COMMON SENSE V. RECONCILEMENT.

Slr,—l rejoice to find Mr. Dignum recognises the friendly spirit of my last note. I may say that I have a great and long-standing respect for him as an upright and conscientous man. And I see no sufficient reason why a difference of opinion should in any degree lessen so satisfactory a state of mind on either side. Let us agree to differ. Mr. Dignum accuses me of "imperfect reasoning:" I will give him another example of my shortcomings in that way, lii my siißilicity, I inferred that when Mr. Dignum Was smiting the critics_idis sssa• ' thigh, both sides of the questie._--,srum nave been shown. Now on the authorits,-."11e ,sayist,l am enabled to say ' that it is not .so, but was altogether a one-sided affair, In avtilA my friend set up the straw-stuffed dummies of the critica and of course quickly knocked the stuffing out of their irresponsive bodies. I do not think my friend Shows better as the smiter of the absent than in the more heroic figure my "imperfect reasonine as- signed to hint However, he has himself to blame for this. Mr. Dignurn is not the first man who, imagining himself the critic, has dispelled that illusion by his own pen. lam really sorry that a constitutional inaptitude for calm and dispassionate controversial treatment should so frequently drag my friend into the quagmire of angry inargurnentative declamation, and impel him to fling about fragments of inappropriate Latin. But Mr. Dignum (perhaps conveniently) has no time to follow "me into the gist of my letter, in which I made a grave charge against him." He tells me it was "irrelevant to his paper." There again I must beg to differ from him. The claim which I have heard my friend make of his right to alter important words used in an impoilant physical statement in the Bible is the basis, the very foundation of his system of dealing with Biblical critics and criticism. On what canon of sound reasoning can this be allowed? Viewed from his own stand-point, the Bible is the Word of God, and I maintain that as such it should be regarded reverently as the last will and testament of the Supreme, and held inviolate,f rat from mutilation and interpolation. Heavy penalties are attached to the sin of altering the wording of human wills, how much more heinous then to tamper with the Divine? But Mr. Dignum's occupation as a critic of the critics. I would be gone were he not allowed the privilege of I tinkering the text to make it fit for the increased dimensions of modern knowledge. Does it not seem rather arrogant on the part of our friend to think that what has been good for the Almighty Inspirer of the Bible, as expressing his will for so many thousands of years should not also be good enough for John Dignum ? Has He, the Omnipotent,the Omnicient, left these grave defects in His word to be corrected by the mighty reconcilers of the nineteenth century? Perhaps it was I foreseen chat in these later days a sect would arise who, though no conjurors, would be able to juggle with the word and fit it to meet modern requirements? And here I am amazed that it should never have struck Mr. Dignum I that, if his view is right, what " blind leaders of the blind" the religious teachers of the last century must have been not to have seen that a dcy with its expressly mentioned evening and morning was not a day, hut something else—anything but a day in fact. Was there this lack of learning, of common sense and common un- derstanding, among the Wegleys, Whitfields, and Clarkes of that day? And this brings me to Mr. John Gandy. This other friend of mine thinks with me that a belief in the dogma ol Redemption is only lleirtallyconsistent,when we enter- tain a belief also in the dogma of the Fall. Where we differ is in his inference that no authority for a belief in these two donnas is to be found in Scripture. He says that Christ Himself never mentions them. Perhaps not specially in those words; but does not the context and tenour of PHs teaching lead us reasonably to infer this? And does not the contrary assumption (i.e. that the Fall and Redemption as essential articles of Christian faith. may he rejected and the rejector still logically regard himself as a Christian) does not this throw the odium of mental obliquity and want of Biblical knowledge upon the good men I have mentioned and others who thought and taught the direct contrary? Mr. Gandy asked me" What is a Christian ?" This, from a profess- ing Chrstian to one outside the pale,is certainly a curious question. But I think my idea of this subject may be gathered from the foregoing remarks. I think a true Christian must believe in the Fall. the Redemption, and in the Divinity of Christ, and strive to follow His ex- ample as closely as he may. Igo with the majority of pulpits in this, and I think its rejection reduces Christ to the position of a mere moral philosopher. There is one idea suggested by both Mr. Dignum's and Mr. Gandy's letter, and that is the human influence modern secular knowledge has had upon the belief in the Bible narratives. How greatly this has modified old- time beliefs the present discussion shows.—! am. &c. JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 15th December, 1890.

div.p: TilE EXAMLN_ER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1890.

BA.ZAAR AND ENTERTAINMENT AT THE RUNCORN BOARD SCFIOOLS. Thursday last, being the "breaking up" claw for the Christmas holidays, was celebrated at the above schools in a novel and pleasing manner. In the afternoon a children's bazaar was held, the proceeds of which were devoted to the "prize fund" of the schools. The stalls were very tastefully laid out by Miss Kilburn, the head mistress, and her assistants, and were in charge of eight girls. They were well filled with both useful and ornamental articles, suitable for childremand the amount of money taken fully testified to that fact. The refreshment stall was well patronised by the boys and girls. Precisely at two o'clock Mr. Hewitt, chair- man of the School Management Committee opened the bazaar with a short but interesting speech. Among those present were Dr. McDougall and Mr. Moss, clerk to the Board. The children were highly delighted with this new treat. Praise is due to Miss Killburn for the very effective manner in which the arrangements were carried out, everything being a de- cided success. In the evening there was given a magic lantern entertainment conisting of Christmas stories, and fairy tales, interspersed with hymns and carols. Mr. Moulton and Miss Kilburn divided the work of explain- ing the views. The number of scholars present was about 600. At the conclusisn each child received an orange, and with cheers for the teachers, members of the Board, and the holidays, the youngsters separated.

div.head: WIDNES AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
div.p: WIDNES AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY.

The members of this Society signalised their fifth season by the production in the Alexandra Theatre on Wednesday evening,Mr.Tom Taylor's well-known comedy, " Still waters run deep." Although the Society has established a reputation for histrionric ability, the audience which assembled was of very meagre proportions,and the beggarly erray of empty bemhes was by no means an inspiring feature. As John Milway,Mr. R. Lewis displayed considerable ability, and sustained with capital effect the character of a man who was " notso queer ashe looked." The impersonation of Captain Hawksley, by Mr. Harry Cookson, was a finished and well sustained piece of acting throughout, and evidenced capabilities of the highest order. Mr. Wm. Kershaw was capitally made up as Mr. Potter and his pourtrayal of a difficult part was a very creditable per- formance. Mr. T. C. Welding was an amusing "Dun- bilk." Mrs. Richard Lewis took the part of Mrs. Hector Sternhold and gave a capital representation of the med- dlesome strong-minded aunt. Miss A. C. Davies made a pleasing and efficient Mrs. Midway. The remaining characters, were Langford, Mr. G. E. Sayce ; Markham, Mr. Herbert White; Gimlet, Mr. Fred W. Wareing; and Tessop, Mr. C. Harold Watson. The play worked smoothly throughout, and the audience were able to follow the plot with no small degree of pleasure and interest. At the close of the performance the prin- ciple characters were called before the curtain, and Mrs. Gossage, who occupied a box, presented Mrs. Lewis and Miss Davies with a beautiful bouquet each.—On Thurs- day evening the comedietta "Withered Leaves" was presented before a fairly large audience. The cast was: Sir Conyers Conyers, Bart Mr. C. Harold Watson Tom Conyers Mr. J. Walwyn White Arthur Middleton Mr. Wm. Kershaw Cecil Vane Mr. Fred. W. Wareing Lady Conyers Miss Robertson May Rivers Miss A. C. Davies Then followed the farce "The Area Belle" the characters being as follow: Pitcher (In the police) Mr. G. E. Sayee Tosser (in the Grenadiers) Mr. C. Harold Watson Walker Chalks (a Milkman) Mr. Herbert White Mrs. Croaker (the" Missus") Miss Robertson
Penelope (the'" Area Belle") Miss Lily Leatherbarrow The acting was again of a high order of merit. Last evening" Still Waters Run Deep "was repeated.

W. Lightbum seconded the motion, and remarked that the day had gone by when they need dilate upon the importance of education. Their position as Commis- sioners was clear. div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

The second concert of the season was held in the Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday night, when the grand oratorio "The Messiah" was performed. llandel's masterpiece appears never to lose its freshness and power to attract. The body of the hail was well filled and there was also a large corn- pan3 in the gallery. The whole of the dress seats had been appropriated. The band and chorus num- bered 150 performers, and the principals were Miss Marianne Fenna, (soprano), Miss Annie Hallwood (contralto), Mr. Edwin Houghton (tenor), and Mr. Lucas Williams (bass). Miss Dews had been engaged to take the contralo solos, but almost at the last moment that lady had telegraphed that she could not fulfil her engagement owing to hoarseness, and Miss Hallwood kindly and promptly consented to fill the vacancy. The absence of Miss Dews was, however, a great disappoint- ment. Dealing first with the choir, which was conducted by the Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, it may justly be said that they acquitted themselves with the utmost credit and ability, the difficult choruses being attacked with precision and vigour, and there was, on the whole, a finish about their work which deserves frank praise. That universal favourite "For unto us a child is born," was a highly enjoyable performance and displayed in no small degree the qualities of the choir. The same may be said of "Lift up your heads," the "Hallelujah Chorus," and "He trusted in God." Miss Fenna, who is the possessor of a voice of pleasing quality, sang the various solo parts alloted to her with the skill of a trained artist, putting adequate expression into the intricate music. Miss Hallwood, who was labouring under the disadvantage of taking the part unprepared, seemed rather unsuited to oratorio work, her vocalisation being too " mechanical " to be effective, although she has a voice of good tone. Her best effort was" He shall feed his flock." The success of the evening was scored by Mr. Houghton. Besides a pure-toned, clear, powerful tenor voice, he has the added gifts of good expression and capital enunciation, and each item was rendered in a manner that was highly effective and enjoyable. Mr. Williams was suffering from a slight cold, and scarcely did himself justice, his vocalisation lacking the requisite vigour and posver. His various solos were, however, rendered tunefully. "The trumpet shall sound" with trumpet obligato by Mr. R. W. Fierpoint was much enjoyed. The band, of which Mr. F. Duncanson was the leader, accompanied through- out with skill and judgment, and the performance of the "pastoral symphony" was a very fine one indeed. The audience was less demonstrative than the Runcorn people usually are, and during the whole evening only two re- calls were made, and Mr. Houghton and Mr. Williams were the two thus distinguished, and bowed their ac- knowledgments.

div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Taylor ire were present Messrs. P. Speak- man, C.C., P. Smith, F. Wiswall, W. Hankinson, J. W. Lightburn, W. Fisher, E. Imison, H. J. Grice, J. Pritchard, E. W. llumphreys, F. A. Lake, (law clerk), and E. Marshall, (secretary).—The substance of the report was as follows:—" Your Committee have the honour to report that they have carefully con- sidered the educational needs of Runcorn, and whether those needs can be supplied under the provisions of the above named Acts. The Denominational Schools and the School Board provide ample accommodation for elemen- tag education, but for education beyond that stage there is no public provision. Some parents send their children to Liverpool and other places at considerable expense, and no doubt there are many other parents who are anxious to give their children a good education, and would be willing to pay for it, if there was a good public school in the town giving a modern commercial and technical education. To such a school scholars frem the elementary school might be admitted after passing through the necessary standards. There is also a lack of provision for Scientific and Techni- cal Education of a more advanced order. It is true that Science and Art classes have,from time to time,been con- ducted as Private adventures on the part of the Teachers, but such Classes have been of a temporary and inter- mittent character, not being connected with any per- manent Institution. Inshort, it may be said that Educa- tion in Runcorn ends with the Elementary School, for want of an Institution to carry it further. After care- fully considering the two Acts before named, we are of opinion that they fully meet the difficulty, and we are unanimous in recommending the formation and establishment of a Technical Institute for the teach- ing of Science and Art and Commercial Subjects. We therefore propose (1) that a building be erected to in- clude a Lecture Dall,and rooms for Manuel and Technical Training; to accommodate from two hundred to two hundred and fifty day pupils. (2.) In this building to give Technical Instruction in three forms in the day school and in the evening school in all such subjects as may promote the Technical, Manual, and Commercial Education in such subjects as the following : SCIENCE. Chemistry, practical and theoretical •, magnetism and electricity; astronomy (elementary) and navigation; geometry, mathematics, and mechanics, pure and applied ; sound, light, heat. ART.—Freehand, model *c., according to South Kensington requirements. TEcumcAr. SUBJECTS. Mechanical engineering ; machine construction ; building construction ; steam ; plumbing ; quantities, surveying, and levelling. Comximmr. SUBJECTS. Shorthand, typewriting; French, Germm, Spanish, Sze. ; commercial calculations; commercial history and geography. Fort GlRLS.—Cooking, hygiene, and dressmaking. The foregoing subjects are suitable to the present and future industries of the town and neighbourhood._

The estimated cost of the buildng is £3,000, not in- eluding purchase of land. The name suggested is "The Runcorn Technical Institute."—Description of principal industries in the district :—Aikali and other chemical manufactures, soap manufacture, shipping and canal traffic, iron foundry, tanning andcurrying, ship building, quarrying, building, rope manufacture, farming, and commercial pursuits. Mr. J. Pritchard moved that the report be received and that application be made to the Cheshire County Council for a building grant, and a grant in support of the annual expenses of a technical school, and also for a grant in aid of the University Extension Lectures to meet the annual deficiency. Mr. Pritchard said the consideration of the Technical Education Act was referred to the Parliamen- tary Committee, and they, wishing for the best possible assistance they could get on the:question, delegated their duties to a sub-coramittee which consisted of certain commissioners, and members of the School Board and Free Library, and the managers of each denominational school in the town. It was a representative committee, and one very capable ot dealing with the education question, and he thought the Board would be satis- fied with the report presented and the scheme sketched out together with the probable advantages to be derived. Up to the present time the advantage of Technical Education Act had not been fully realised, but the country, was now awakening to the importance of the vast benefits that may be derived from the application of the Technical Instruction Act. In addition to providing secondary education, the object of Technical Instruction Act was to provide training for the eye and for the hand. The expression manual labour meant instruction in the use of tools, the pro- cesses of agriculture, and modelling in clay and other materials. Boys wider such circumstances could be shown how to work in wood and the use of tools, tic., but they could not be taught a trade. Mr. Pritchard explained that in consequence of the Local Taxation Act the County Council were in possession of £13,500 to de- vote to technical instruction in the county,and the Board did a wise thing when a month ago they made applica- tion to the County Council to return an amount which they thought, the Commissioners were entitled to. The Commissioners aaould now make another urgent appeal to the County Cauncil, for a building grant from the funds at its disposal for the furtherance of technical edu- cation. A further building grant could be obtained from the Department of Science and Art, and, with the assist- ance from other sources, there ought not to be much difficulty in raising the necessary amount of a techni- cal school, waieli might be roughly estimated at £3,000. div.head: BREACH OF PROMISE CASE OF LOCAL INTEREST.
div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE CASE OF LOCAL INTEREST.

A breach of promise action came on for hearing on Monday before Mr. Edwin Gray, Under Sheriff of York, and a jury, at the Town Hall, Leeds, in which the plain- tiff was Henrietta Reynolds, assistant milliner, residing with her parents at Wakefield, and the defendant Albert Haynes, draper, Alderly Edge. The breach being ad- mitted the court had before it simply the question of damages. Mr. Beverley, barrister, was for the plaintiff, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Salomonson, ' solicitor, of Wilmslow.—Mr. Beverley said when the promise occurred plaintiff was an assistant with her sister, and earning 15s. a week. The parties seemed to have met together at Warrington, about five years ago. De- fendant at that time was an apprentice, but he was now aged 25 years,and the plaintiff was 23 years of age. They at once took a liking to each other, and the courtship be- gan. After a little while the plaintiff's parents removed to Wakefield, and she went with them. Defendant con- tinued to visit her at Wakefield, and occasionally staved at her house. It was in fact a properly constituted and recognized courtship. No formal engagament was entered into until the end of 1887,and they appeared by that time to have carefully thought over the matter. It would appear from the correspondence that the defendant was by no means one of those gushing young men who fell in and out of love as a moth fell into a candle flame. He de- liberately and carefully made a proposal to the plaintiff and ha was accepted. It was subsequently arranged that the marriage shotild take place in February of the pre- sent year. In 1888 the plaintiff and her mother went to visit some friends first going to Warrington and then to Manchester and Liverpool, to all of which places the de- fendant followed her. Correspondence went on until 1889, when they found a little bit of romance brought in- to the affair in the shape of poetry. He could not resist the following, which he supposed defendant believed to be true:— What is love, that all the world thinks so much about It? What is love, that neither you nor I can do without It? Love's a tyrant and a slave, a torment and a pleasure ; And having it, we know no peace. Lacking it we know no pleasure. Would we shun it if we could? I thoroughly doubt it. would rather bear its pain than live my life without it. Mr. Beverley, resuming his remarks, said that after that effusion, he did try to see how he could "live with- out it," because they found that in January of this year he commenced to sign himself "Yours truly, A. Haynes," while In other letters he had concluded with the words "Yours lovingly," "Yours for ever." " Your loving Albert," and so on. The plaintiff was called, and bore out the counsel's statements in its main particulars. She said she had given defendant no occasion whatever to break off the engagement. She had sent him several presents, including a dressing-ease, and he had not acknowledged the last one. She was under the doctor's care for three months.—The defendant was called, and stated that as to his position he was in business at Alderly Edge, and rented a £3O shop. He started a month or two ago with £2OO capital, lent by his uncle, without any security. His takings were about £lO a week. He had no interest in a leather factory.—The jury having been addressed in the interests of both parties,the Under-sheriff summed up, and after deliberating for a few minutes, the jury gave a verdict for the plaintiff, with damages £9O.

- _ Canon Molesworth, the late vicar of St. Clement's Church, Rochdale, and the author of a history of Eng- the Church of England, and other land, a history of works, died at his residence in Rochdale yesterday morn- ing. He was in his severay-fourth year: a‘nd ever since the spring of Ina his health has gradually declined. Congestion of' the lungs set in on Tuesday last, and his recovery was hopeless.

THE KILKENNY CONTEST. Messrs. Sexton and Justin McCarthy addressed a meeting at Kilkenny. A great number .of priests in Kilkenny, are canvassing on behalf of'Sir Phpe Hennessy. Mr. Parnell and his friends addressed meetings yesterday. Mr. Michael Da vitt telegraphs :—"'lt is absolutely false that lime was thrown into Mr. Parnell's face. The facts are that some women and young' girls pelted him with flour and mud. There was not a particle of limain the place." ANOTHER RAILWAY COLLISION.

Another collision occurred at seven o'clock yesterday morning between two empty passenger trains, outside London Bridge Station, on the London, Brigirton, and South Coast line. The permanent way was torn up for about twenty yards, and a third-class carriage was wrecked, but the officials sustained no injury. Traffic on the Mid-Kent line from New Cross to Canal Bridge, was blocked. The Bricklayers' Arms Goods Depot was also blocked, and the lino cannot he cleared for some time. Another report says that 'me of the trains was filled with workmen, anclit ran into an empty passenger train in front of it. None of the occupants of the work- men's train were injured; but all traffic oil the line was stopped all morning.

TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA. LOSS OF LIFE: MANY INJURED. A terrible railway occident accurred near Quebec, on Thursday at mid-day. The west-bound express from Halifax to Montreal was crossing the bridge over theriver at St. Joseph de Levis, opposite the city when the stmc- tore suddenly collapsed, and the entire train, except the engine and baggage car,, fell through into the water and submerged. NEW YORE, Frmiay.—Later intelligence from St. Joseph states that 35 persons are known to have been injured by the accident on, a railway bridge yesterday ' while an express train waacrossirw. Of these several are so seriously hurt that their lives, are despaired of. Many more who were injured have been hurriedly removed from the scene to their homes or to places of shelter in the vicinity, and these are not included in the numbers already given. It is feared that three more dead bodies lies under the debris at the bridge, and this would lazing the total of killed up to eight.

—.— - The enthronement of the Bishop of Bangor took place yesterday-, at Bangor Chthedral , the ceremony being per- formed by the buffragan Bishop of Dover.
THE WEATHER.-DEEP SNOW.

A deep mantle of snow lies over the metropolis. From all parts of the country come reports of the severity of the weather, with gales and heavy fall of snow. THE QUEEN'S DEPARTURE FO OSBORNE. The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice, Prince Henry of Battenburgh, and the Royal suite, left Windsor yesterday mornin7, for Osborne. During the journey snow lay thickly on the ground, and the air was keen.

THE NORTH-EASTERN RAILWAY- DIMUTE. Mr. Harford, secretary of the workmen, has, says our Newcastle correspondent, informed the directors of the North-Eastern Railway that the men will appointthree of their numberto wait upon the directors with plenary powers to settlethe present dispute. • TWO VESSELS WRECKED'. During the strong gale from ,northward yesterday morning, the ketch Endeavour, from Newport to Bode, with coal, was driven on the rocks under aillsborough Hill,, near Ilfracombe, and went to pieces. The crew were saved. The barque Oregon, of Dundee. from Iquique, is supposed to have foundered off Salcombe. The crew were saved. THE CARDIFF TRAGEDY'. Yesterday at the Glamorgan Asszies, at Swasea, David Harsent was charged with murdering a' woman named Roderick at Cardiff, and with shooting her husband with intent to murder. The Rodericks had complhined, of the prisoner's cruelty, and lie thereupon shot them. Evi- dence showed that the prisoner was insane„ and he was accordingly ordered to be confined during her Majesty's pieasure.. DEATH OF CANON MOLESWORTH.

div.head: PHONOGRAPH AT THE IUnLIC' HALL
div.p: THE PHONOGRAPH AT THE IUnLIC' HALL

On Thursday evening a tfemonstraticrt of the wonderful capacity for reproc7nOing sounds' of Edi- sen's latest phonograph was given in the Public Hall, Warrington, by Mr. W. Lyhd. M.1.E.1.1 Mr. Robert Garnett presided. The attendance vem.4 not very large, a circumstance no doubt due to the cold , and unfavourable weather, and other attractiMag in the town on the same evening. The Chairman hi a few introductory remarks, said the greatest book that had been published in this century was the book of Stanley's on "Darkest A frica," and the ffext greatest was General Booth's on "Darkest Ei- land." It was one of the signs of thetimes of to-dhy that the public of this land were taking an interest ' not only in the working classes bat also in th;e. class that is a great deal below them*,—the men who, were willing to work but had not got any work too, do. He was sure they all rejoiced to see the efforts* that were being put forth to raise fallen humanity. The great purpose for which they ought to li'Ve was that the world might be better for their living M it. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to the meetings held during the week at St. Helens and Liverpool, in support of General Booth's scheme, he said that in Warrington they had no agencies far those charitable purposes. The great question the Saviour asked them was, "'What do ye more than others ?" and that question camehnme to them In full force, for he did not think they were doing as much as others. There were schemes actively working in Manchester and Liverpool, and it was on behalf of one of those schemes that Professor Lynd had come to War- rington that night, the proceeds of that 'meeting going directly to the support of the mission held' in the Central Hall, Manchester. (Hear, hear.)=-Iffi: Lynd then gave a brief but lucid account of the con- struction of the phonograph and its mode of ' working. He also alluded to the numeious uses to which the instrument could be put in recording music of all kinds, in taking down and reproducing speeches, and for correspondence. After this he gave a, selection of instrumental and vocal music which had been taken down weeks or months ago in distant parts of the coun- try by the phonograph, on the wax cylinders which are used for the purpose. These musical sounds were repro- duced with wonderful faithfulness and were distinctly heard in all parts of the hall. To show its use itreorres- pondence, Mr. Lynd also dictated to the pnonograph a business'letter and a love letter, the love letter beginning with a very audible sigh and ending with kisses. These letters, sighs and kisses inclusive, were then repeated by the machine with a clearness which highly 'astonished,' and amused the audience. On the invitation of the lecturer, the Chairman, Mr. T. Morris, and Mi. John Walker, spoke a few sentences into the phonograph an d these too were directly after faithfully reproduced. The lecture and exhibition were much enjoyed by the. audience whose applause was frequent and hearty.
